novelty.remaining_novel_angle:
The high-level framing is already published. 'Allocate bits and cameras by expected synthesised-view distortion over the viewer's navigation distribution' is the IMVS / VSD literature (Toni, Frossard, Ortega; 3D-HEVC VSO). 'Viewer-culling bandwidth apportioning across live multi-camera RGB-D 2D-codec streams' is LiVo (CoNEXT 2025). 'Learned pre- and post-processors around standard codecs trained with a novel-view loss' is Sandwiched RGB-D. 'A flicker regulariser inside a rate-distortion loss' is PD-4DGS and V^3. 'Don't resend static regions' is DeltaStream and LiveVV.

The defensible novelty is narrower, and has three parts:
(a) Treat temporal flicker of the rendered novel view as a first-class coding objective for the input RGB-D streams of a stateful, learned IBR renderer (rate + λ·view-distortion + μ·flicker, measured after TSDF fusion and blending). That includes the first empirical characterisation of how depth-codec noise, GOP/QP/intra-refresh choices and TSDF temporal state interact to produce flicker. No found work measures flicker for codec-coded RGB-D feeding IBR: Sandwiched RGB-D is frame-independent with no temporal metric, and ReVo/LiVo report only SSIM/MOS.
(b) Use a learned renderer's blend weights × alpha, back-projected into source cameras and integrated over a predicted HMD-pose distribution, as a differentiable per-CTU sensitivity in place of analytic DIBR VSD models. This is a modest but concrete upgrade over VSD and LiVo-style culling, contingent on LiVo's full text not already using a rendered-quality model.
(c) Reuse the receiver's persistent TSDF/background state as both a skip or concealment model and a flicker suppressor, with confidence-gated refresh. This is distinct from DeltaStream's change-detection deltas because what may be skipped is decided by what the receiver's renderer can already explain.

A reviewer will see (b) alone as incremental over VSD/IMVS plus LiVo. The paper needs (a) as its headline, with (b) and (c) as mechanisms.
novelty.best_variant:
Idea 2 ('Consistency Is Compressible'), extended with Idea 1's blend-weight sensitivity map, has the most defensible novelty. Its distinctive claim is that codec-induced depth noise is a major, unmeasured source of flicker in stateful geometry-guided IBR, and that sender-side temporal filtering plus rate-distortion-flicker training of sandwich pre- and post-processors reduces bitrate and flicker together. None of the found prior work does this: Sandwiched RGB-D is per-frame with no temporal metric, PD-4DGS and V^3 add flicker only on the representation side, and LiVo, ReVo and DeltaStream report no flicker. The characterisation study is itself publishable at MM or TCSVT.

Idea 1 as a standalone systems paper (MobiCom/NSDI/CoNEXT) is riskier, for three reasons:
- Its core allocation idea is the IMVS/VSD formulation with a learned renderer substituted in.
- LiVo, from a group with exactly this rate-allocation expertise (Ortega, Govindan), already owns 'bandwidth-adaptive live multi-camera RGB-D conferencing with viewer culling' at CoNEXT 2025.
- Winning would need large measured BD-rate and flicker gains over a faithful LiVo re-implementation.

The recommended combination has two parts:
- Headline: a rate-distortion-flicker objective and the characterisation of how codec noise turns into flicker through the TSDF state.
- Mechanisms: per-CTU QP from renderer sensitivity, and TSDF-state-based skipping.

Before committing, get the LiVo full text (ACM open access returned 403 here) and check whether its bandwidth apportioning already uses a rendered-view quality model.

sharpened.title: Consistency Is Compressible: Rate-Distortion-Flicker Coding of Multi-Camera RGB-D for Stateful Geometry-Guided View Synthesis
sharpened.one_liner: Lossy coding of depth, not the renderer, is the largest source of flicker in rendered novel views when RGB-D telepresence runs at realistic bitrates. This project measures that effect, then codes the RGB-D inputs against a rate + view-distortion + flicker objective computed after TSDF fusion and blending. It moves temporal consistency to the sender and uses the renderer's back-projected blend weights to decide where depth bits go.
sharpened.core_claim:
Falsifiable claim, in two parts.
(i) Characterisation. Setting: 4-8 camera RGB-D telepresence at 5-30 Mbit/s total, coded with HEVC or AV1 in low-delay settings. At these rates, codec-induced depth error causes most (at least 50%) of the increase in rendered novel-view temporal error (flow-warping error / tOF) relative to rendering from uncompressed inputs. A receiver-side temporal depth filter, such as the base paper's colour-gated filter, removes less than half of this increase, because it cannot tell codec noise from motion.
(ii) Remedy. The system combines sender-side temporal pre-filtering, per-CTU depth QP from renderer sensitivity, and a small recurrent post-filter trained with a flicker term. Against plain codec + base renderer, it achieves at least 25% BD-rate saving at matched rendered flicker and at least 10% at matched LPIPS. Against a per-frame Sandwiched-RGB-D-style pre/post-processor at matched rate, it gives at least 20% lower flicker. The whole system stays standard-codec compliant and adds less than 5 ms per frame.
If (i) fails, the paper does not exist. If (ii) holds only at matched LPIPS and not at matched flicker, the work collapses into VSO/Sandwiched and should be dropped.
sharpened.key_insight:
In a stateful IBR pipeline (per-view splats, then temporal depth filter + image-based TSDF, then blend network), temporal consistency and compressibility are aligned.
- A depth video that has been temporally stabilised at the sender, using the same TSDF/static-region state the receiver would compute, has lower temporal entropy. It is therefore cheaper to code, and it leaves no codec noise for the receiver to mistake for motion.
- The coding error that remains should be shaped, not minimised uniformly. Error is harmless where the renderer gives a pixel little weight (low blend weight × alpha, back-projected to the source) or where the TSDF is already well supported. It is harmful at silhouettes and in newly dynamic regions, where it flips which pixel wins the opaque splat and produces temporal pops.
- 3D-HEVC VSO/VSD models this spatially for analytic DIBR. Nobody models it temporally for a learned renderer with persistent state. Because codec GOP structure (I-frame pumping, intra-refresh, QP cascades) is itself temporal, flicker is a coding decision, not just a rendering artefact.
sharpened.method:
Stage 0. Characterisation harness (the main contribution; also released as a benchmark).
- Content: multi-view sequences with sensor or estimated depth.
- Coding: x265 / SVT-AV1 / NVENC in low-delay P, with sweeps over QP, GOP length, intra-refresh versus periodic IDR, depth bit-depth packing (8-bit inverse depth vs 10/12-bit, Starline-style luma packing), and colour/depth rate split.
- Rendering: at held-out rig cameras AND along synthetic head-motion trajectories between rig cameras. Both use the base pipeline, or a faithful re-implementation (Starline-style image-based TSDF + 4-level blend U-Net) if base code is unavailable.
- Decomposition: rendered flicker split into renderer-intrinsic, depth-codec and colour-codec parts by swapping inputs.

Stage 1. Sender-side consistency pre-filter.
- Run the temporal depth filter and a lightweight confidence net at the sender, before encoding.
- Encode the stabilised depth plus an optional 1-bit, run-length-coded silhouette/edge side channel.
- Budget: at most 3 ms on the sender GPU.

Stage 2. Renderer-sensitivity rate control.
- For M sampled target poses (the rig's held-out cameras, or a predicted viewer-pose cloud), run only the cheap forward-splat and weight stage. Back-project w·alpha into each source camera.
- Accumulate per-CTU sensitivity maps separately for depth (weighted by silhouette proximity and dynamic mask) and for colour.
- Map sensitivity to per-CTU delta-QP with a closed-form Lagrangian rule. The rule is calibrated offline by fitting d(LPIPS + μ·flicker)/d(rate) per sensitivity bin, a learned R-D slope regressor with fewer than 50k params.
- Delivery: x265 --qpfile/zones or NVENC QP-delta maps. No decoder change.

Stage 3. Recurrent post-filter at the receiver.
- A small ConvGRU (at most 0.5 GMAC per view) on decoded depth, conditioned on decoded colour and the receiver's previous fused TSDF depth warped into the source view.
- Trained through a differentiable codec proxy: a learned HEVC/AV1 proxy in the style of Sandwiched, with straight-through real-codec forward passes in the last epochs to limit mismatch.
- The frozen base renderer sits inside the loss:
  L = λ·R_est + L1/LPIPS(novel view) + μ·||W_{t←t-1}(I_{t-1}) − I_t||_occ (flow-warped temporal error on rendered novel views, flow from RAFT on GT) + η·depth-edge loss.
- Optional variant: jointly train a pre-processor (full Sandwiched style) to show that the temporal term, not the sandwich, gives the gain.

Training data:
- DNA-Rendering and MVHumanNet (multi-view humans; depth from off-the-shelf MVS/stereo FM).
- Panoptic Studio Kinect sequences (real ToF depth).
- Held-out test on DyNeRF / ENeRF-Outdoor / D3DMV (the base paper's protocol) plus Panoptic.

Runtime budget:
- Sender: at most 5 ms added.
- Receiver: at most 5 ms added on an RTX 4090-class GPU, measured end to end with real encode/decode.
sharpened.why_not_engineering:
1. It makes a measurable scientific claim that is currently unknown and could come out either way: how much of the flicker in rendered telepresence is caused by coding, and whether receiver-side temporal machinery can undo it. Nobody has measured this. Sandwiched RGB-D is per-frame with no temporal metric, and LiVo/ReVo report SSIM/MOS only. DSGS (arXiv 2605.17002) even reports the opposite effect, compression stabilising splat prediction, for texture-only atlases. So the outcome is uncertain, and the uncertainty can be resolved.
2. It introduces a new optimisation target, rate + view-distortion + flicker measured after a stateful renderer. Its gradient w.r.t. source-pixel coding error is derived from the renderer itself. This replaces spatial-only analytic VSD with a temporal, learned-renderer sensitivity.
3. It reverses a design assumption in the base paper, that temporal filtering belongs at the receiver, and shows the reversal is better on both rate and flicker.

Per-CTU QP maps and WebRTC plumbing are delivery mechanisms, not the contribution.
sharpened.differentiation:
- vs Sandwiched RGB-D (arXiv 2404.09979) and Sandwiched Video (2303.11473, 2407.07395): these process frames independently, use a warp/JPEG proxy, and have no temporal loss or metric and no TSDF state. We add a flicker term measured after a stateful renderer, a recurrent post-filter that uses receiver state, and sender-side consistency. The flicker gain is shown at matched rate, and an ablation re-trains Sandwiched with and without our temporal term.
- vs 3D-HEVC VSO/VSD and region-based VSD estimation (arXiv 2510.17037): these are analytic, spatial-only, two-view DIBR models. We compare directly against HTM VSO-coded depth and show it does not reduce rendered flicker.
- vs IMVS navigation-aware allocation (arXiv 1802.08994): that work selects views at per-view granularity for pre-encoded content. We make only intra-stream CTU-level decisions in live low-delay coding, and pose-distribution integration is optional, not the headline.
- vs LiVo (CoNEXT 2025, doi 10.1145/3768981): LiVo apportions bandwidth across streams and culls out-of-view content. Its full text was inaccessible, so whether its allocation uses a rendered-quality model is unverified; the team must read it before submission. We do not claim cross-stream apportioning as new. We use a LiVo-style frustum-cull + stream-split allocator as a baseline and add our intra-stream sensitivity and flicker objective on top.
- vs PD-4DGS (arXiv 2605.11427), V^3 (arXiv 2409.13648), 4DGC: these put flicker or temporal terms into representation-side coding of offline 4DGS. We code live RGB-D inputs for a feed-forward renderer.
- vs DeltaStream (MobiSys 2025) and LiveVV (arXiv 2310.08205): these send change-detected deltas. We do not claim skipping. Receiver-state-aware skipping is left to a follow-up systems paper.
- vs DSGS (arXiv 2605.17002) and GS-SCNet (arXiv 2604.25330): these are alternative wire formats (texture-only atlases, semantic latents). They are included as anchors where code allows, and the DSGS 'compression stabilises' finding is explicitly tested in the RGB-D setting.

datasets: CMU Panoptic Studio: the only large public multi-view set with real synchronised Kinect RGB-D (10 Kinect v2). Used for real ToF noise and for flying pixels under codec error. Verify the depth/colour calibration tooling (panoptic-toolbox).

DyNeRF / Neural 3D Video: 18-21 cams, 300 frames per scene. Depth from the base pipeline's stereo/MVS or a stereo foundation model. Matches the base paper's protocol; evaluate all 300 frames, not only the first 100.
ENeRF-Outdoor and D3DMV: the base paper's other test sets. D3DMV is already compressed (640x360), so report it separately as a 'double-compression' case.
DNA-Rendering and MVHumanNet: many-camera human captures used to train the post-filter and the R-D slope regressor, with pseudo depth from MVS.

Optional custom capture: 4-6 Azure Kinect / Orbbec Femto Bolt around a seated talker, 2-3 minute conversations, plus 2 held-out RGB cams. About $3-5k. It is not strictly required, but reviewers at IEEE VR/MM will value real telepresence-style ToF content, and minute-long sequences are needed to test drift under long GOPs.
baselines: Uniform HEVC/AV1 (x265, SVT-AV1, NVENC low-delay) of all RGB and depth streams, followed by the unmodified base pipeline (Starline-like anchor)
MV-HEVC / 3D-HEVC HTM with VSO-enabled depth coding (the analytic VSD rate-control anchor)
Receiver-only temporal filtering: the base paper's colour-gated filter + TSDF feedback on decoded depth (tests whether receiver state already removes codec flicker)
A post-hoc video deflicker or temporal consistency method applied to the rendered output (e.g. a blind video temporal-consistency network)
Sandwiched RGB-D-style per-frame pre/post-processors, re-trained with the same renderer in the loss but without the temporal term
LiVo-style allocation: frustum culling + dynamic colour/depth stream split, re-implemented from the paper once the full text is obtained
Wire-format anchors where code is available: DSGS-style texture-only atlas + decoder-side splat prediction, and GS-SCNet (human stereo subset only)
metrics: BD-rate at matched novel-view quality: PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS and IV-PSNR at held-out cameras

BD-rate at matched flicker, the headline metric: flow-warping error on rendered novel views (occlusion-masked, flow from ground truth), tOF / tLP, temporal IV-PSNR, and a newly reported 'BD-flicker' at matched rate

Flicker along moving-viewpoint trajectories (synthetic head paths interpolated between rig cameras, plus recorded HMD traces if available), with no ground truth, using warping error between consecutive rendered frames
Flicker decomposition (renderer-intrinsic vs depth-codec vs colour-codec) obtained by input swapping
Depth-edge error and flying-pixel rate at silhouettes
End-to-end added latency (sender pre-filter + sensitivity computation, receiver post-filter) and codec encode/decode times on a stated GPU

Small perceptual study: 2AFC flicker preference on 16-20 subjects at 3 bitrates, including stereo HMD playback of rendered trajectories, used to validate that the objective flicker metrics rank conditions correctly
key_ablations: Sender-side vs receiver-side vs both temporal filtering, at matched rate
With vs without the flicker term (μ=0) in post-filter training
Sensitivity QP source: renderer blend weight × alpha vs frustum-only vs 3D-HEVC VSO vs saliency vs uniform

Codec structure: GOP length, periodic IDR vs gradual intra refresh, and depth packing (8-bit inverse depth vs 10-bit vs Starline luma packing), each measured against rendered flicker (the characterisation core)
Recurrent post-filter conditioning on previous TSDF depth vs no state
Proxy-codec training vs straight-through real-codec fine-tuning (proxy mismatch)
Generalisation of the sensitivity map to a second renderer (e.g. GPS-Gaussian or a simple Starline TSDF without a blend net)
Pose-distribution integration (M sampled poses with prediction noise) vs held-out-camera-only sensitivity
experiments.capture_notes:
Custom capture is not strictly needed. Panoptic Studio gives real multi-Kinect depth, and DyNeRF, ENeRF-Outdoor, D3DMV and DNA-Rendering give multi-view colour, with depth estimated as in the base paper.

The gaps are:
- no public telepresence-style set (seated talker, ToF sensors, minutes long) with held-out cameras;
- no public set of head-tracked viewer trajectories for these scenes.

A small rig (4-6 Azure Kinect or Femto Bolt plus 2 RGB witness cams, about $3-5k, 2-3 weeks of capture engineering) plus 10-20 recorded Quest 3 viewing traces would strengthen an IEEE VR/MM submission and could be released as a benchmark. It should be scheduled after the 2-week test passes, not before.

Also check early whether the base paper's code and weights are public. If they are not, budget about 3-4 weeks to re-implement a Starline-style image-based TSDF + 4-level blend U-Net as the frozen renderer. This is sufficient for the claim, because the claim concerns stateful geometry-guided IBR in general.

review.first_two_week_test:
A no-learning characterisation plus two oracle interventions, on two DyNeRF scenes (e.g. flame_steak, coffee_martini; all 300 frames) and one Panoptic Kinect sequence.

Setup:
- Days 1-3: get the renderer running (base code, or a Starline-style image-based TSDF + simple view-weighted blending, which is enough for the test). Get depth per camera: DyNeRF from an off-the-shelf multi-view stereo / stereo foundation model; Panoptic from raw Kinect.
- Days 4-6: encode depth (and colour) with x265 low-delay P at 5 QPs × {GOP 30 with IDR, infinite GOP with intra-refresh}. Render held-out cameras and 2 synthetic moving trajectories. Measure LPIPS and occlusion-masked flow-warping error of the rendered video against (a) ground truth and (b) the render from uncompressed inputs.
- Decompose flicker by swapping in uncompressed depth or colour.

Oracle interventions (days 7-11):
- (1) Sender-side pre-filter: run the temporal depth filter before encoding, versus the same filter at the receiver on decoded depth, at matched bitrate.
- (2) Oracle sensitivity QP: compute blend-weight × alpha maps from the held-out cameras, back-project to sources, convert to per-CTU delta-QP via x265 --qpfile/zones with a hand-tuned linear rule, versus uniform QP at matched rate.

Days 12-14: compute BD-rate at matched flicker and at matched LPIPS.

Success signal (proceed):
- Depth-codec flicker makes up at least 40-50% of the rendered-flicker increase at 5-30 Mbit/s.
- Receiver-only filtering leaves at least half of it.
- The two untrained interventions together give at least 15% BD-rate at matched flicker.

Any trained component would then add on top of these.
review.kill_criteria:
Drop or pivot if any of the following holds.
1. At realistic telepresence rates (5-30 Mbit/s for 4-8 cams, QP 22-37), depth-codec error causes less than 25% of rendered-flicker increase, i.e. flicker is dominated by the renderer or the blend-net itself. In that case, pivot to a renderer-side temporal-training paper instead.
2. The base paper's receiver-side colour-gated filter + TSDF feedback already removes more than 70% of codec-induced flicker at matched rate.
3. Sender-side pre-filtering + oracle sensitivity QP together give less than 10% BD-rate at matched flicker AND less than 10% flicker reduction at matched rate, meaning shaping doesn't beat uniform coding.
4. 3D-HEVC HTM with VSO already matches the sensitivity-QP gains on flicker, in which case the learned-renderer sensitivity adds nothing over analytic VSD.
5. The LiVo full text (to be read by week 2) turns out to already use a rendered-view distortion model with temporal terms for intra-stream allocation. In that case, drop the rate-control claim and keep only the characterisation (MM short paper / QoMEX).
6. The recurrent post-filter trained with the flicker term fails to beat the per-frame Sandwiched-style variant by at least 15% in flicker at matched rate on held-out scenes. The paper then collapses to a characterisation study only.

reviewer_objections.objection: This is 3D-HEVC VSO/VSD plus Sandwiched compression with a newer renderer swapped in, so the novelty is incremental.
reviewer_objections.rebuttal: VSO/VSD is spatial-only and analytic for two-view DIBR, and Sandwiched RGB-D is frame-independent with no temporal metric. The headline is temporal. We measure, for the first time, how codec GOP/QP/intra-refresh choices propagate through a persistent TSDF state into rendered flicker, and we show that neither HTM-VSO nor per-frame Sandwiched reduces it. Both are included as baselines, and Sandwiched is re-trained with our temporal term as an ablation, so the source of the gain is isolated.

reviewer_objections.objection: The flicker metrics (warping error, tOF) are not validated perceptually, and moving-viewpoint flicker has no ground truth.
reviewer_objections.rebuttal: We report several complementary metrics (masked flow-warping error, tOF/tLP, temporal IV-PSNR) and validate their ranking with a 2AFC study on 16-20 subjects, including stereo HMD playback. For moving viewpoints we use consecutive-frame warping error of the rendered video, with the renderer's own TSDF geometry for the warp, and compare it against uncompressed-input renders as the reference. Recent QA work (GScomp-QA, the compression-vs-temporal-consistency study arXiv 2605.18378) motivates exactly this gap.

reviewer_objections.objection: The results are tied to one specific renderer (Ha et al.), and the sensitivity maps and post-filter may not transfer.
reviewer_objections.rebuttal: Sensitivity is defined for any renderer whose forward pass exposes per-source contribution (blend weights, splat alphas), or via gradients otherwise. We evaluate on two renderers: the base pipeline or a Starline-style TSDF, and a feed-forward Gaussian renderer such as GPS-Gaussian. We also report cross-renderer transfer of the QP rule. The characterisation part does not depend on the renderer.

reviewer_objections.objection: Training through a differentiable codec proxy does not reflect real codec behaviour, and deployment needs standard decoders and low latency.
reviewer_objections.rebuttal: All reported numbers use real x265/SVT-AV1/NVENC bitstreams in low-delay configurations. The proxy is used only for gradients, followed by straight-through fine-tuning with the real codec in the forward pass. Rate control uses standard QP-map interfaces, so the bitstream stays standard compliant. We measure and report sender and receiver overheads (under 5 ms each) and full encode/decode latency on a stated GPU.

reviewer_objections.objection: Why send RGB-D at all? Gaussian/latent wire formats (GS-SCNet, Tele360, DSGS) avoid depth coding, and LiVo already does bandwidth-adaptive RGB-D conferencing.
reviewer_objections.rebuttal: Deployed and research systems still send RGB-D or geometry over 2D codecs (Starline luma-packed depth, ReVo, LiVo), because of hardware codecs and RTC transport. We include DSGS/GS-SCNet as anchors where code allows and test the DSGS 'compression stabilises' finding in the RGB-D setting. For LiVo, we do not claim cross-stream apportioning or culling. A LiVo-style allocator is a baseline, and our intra-stream, flicker-aware shaping composes with it.

effort.months: 6-8 (about 1 month for renderer and harness, 1.5 for characterisation, 3 for the learned post-filter, R-D regressor and ablations, 1-1.5 for the user study and writing). Add about 1 month if custom capture is included.
effort.people: 1 PhD student full-time plus 1 part-time co-author with video-coding or systems background (codec configuration, HTM-VSO baseline, latency measurement)
effort.compute: 2-4 GPUs (RTX 4090 or A100 class). Codec sweeps are CPU-heavy (x265/HTM), so a 32-64 core CPU node helps. Post-filter training takes about 1-3 GPU-days per configuration. Optional $3-5k RGB-D sensor rig plus a Quest 3 for trace recording and the user study.

review.venue: Primary: ACM Multimedia 2027 (main track), where codec-in-the-loop and QoE work with a characterisation study fits best. Alternatives: IEEE VR 2027 / TVCG, if the head-tracked trajectory evaluation and stereo HMD user study are strong; IEEE TCSVT for an extended journal version. CVPR is plausible only if the learned R-D-flicker post-filter shows large, clean gains across two renderers. Treat it as a stretch, since the contribution reads as compression + telepresence. A follow-up systems paper (pose-predictive allocation + receiver-state skipping over WebRTC) would target MMSys/NOSSDAV or CoNEXT, but only after a careful comparison with LiVo.
review.synergies:
1. Persistent-state / wire-format directions (a static-region TSDF or Gaussian state that is sent once, with residuals streamed afterwards). The sender-side pre-filter and receiver-state post-filter here are the first step. Together they make a two-paper series: (a) this RDF characterisation and coding paper, then (b) a receiver-state-aware skip/concealment + pose-predictive allocation systems paper.
2. Head-tracked evaluation benchmarks (moving-viewpoint + dynamic-scene flicker, HMD traces). The moving-trajectory flicker metrics and recorded traces are shared infrastructure and could be released together.
3. Foundation-model or sensor-prompted depth for rigs (Prompt Depth Anything, StreamTTO). Learned depth has different error statistics under compression than ToF, and running the characterisation over both depth sources strengthens both papers.
4. Renderer-side temporal training (adding a temporal loss to the blend net). The flicker decomposition tells that line how much flicker is intrinsic versus caused by the inputs.
5. Perceptual QA of telepresence flicker (a small subjective dataset), with the user study doubling as a dataset contribution.
6. Foveated / gaze-driven coding and loss resilience (ReVo-style FEC). The sensitivity maps extend naturally to gaze weighting and to prioritising FEC for high-sensitivity CTUs.

name: Latency-compensated forecasting of live 3D video (geometry-grounded 3D motion forecasting, audio-conditioned mouth)

cited_work_check.title: Towards Generative Predictive Display for Vision-Based Teleoperation: A Zero-Shot Benchmark of Off-the-Shelf Video Models (Khalil & Kwon, 2026)
cited_work_check.note: Confirmed. It is a zero-shot benchmark of 2D video models for predictive display on CARLA. It concludes that no model is at once accurate, non-divergent and real-time. It has no 3D and no multi-view data.

cited_work_check.title: Streaming Real-Time Rendered Scenes as 3D Gaussians (Siekkinen & Kamarainen, 2026)
cited_work_check.note: Confirmed. It streams a live 3DGS model of server-rendered content (with rigid dynamics) so clients can compensate viewpoint latency. It does not forecast the future motion of captured dynamic content.

cited_work_check.title: NoPo4D: Feed-Forward Dynamic Gaussians from Unposed Multi-View Videos (2026)
cited_work_check.note: Confirmed. It predicts Gaussian velocities, split into image-plane shift plus depth change, for reconstruction and interpolation within the observed time window, not for causal forecasting.

cited_work_check.title: Mon3tr: Monocular 3D Telepresence with Pre-built Gaussian Avatars as Amortization (2026)
cited_work_check.note: The paper exists and is an avatar-based telepresence system. The abstract reports about 80 ms end-to-end latency, not the 73 ms the ideator quotes. It does not forecast motion. The error is minor and numeric only.

cited_work_check.title: Forecasting Future Videos from Novel Views via Disentangled 3D Scene Representation (VEST, ECCV 2024)
cited_work_check.note: Confirmed. It lifts monocular driving video to 3D point clouds, forecasts ego-motion and residual object motion, and renders future frames from novel views. It is offline and has no audio or telepresence. Note that it already shows 3D-lifted forecasting beats entangled 2D forecasting, which undercuts that part of the cluster's claimed insight.

cited_work_check.title: Audio Driven Real-Time Facial Animation for Social Telepresence (SIGGRAPH Asia 2025)
cited_work_check.note: Confirmed. It drives photoreal 3D face avatars from audio with an online, causal transformer (<15 ms GPU time) and no future-audio dependency. It does not forecast captured video and has no latency-hiding framing.

cited_work_check.title: Towards Real-Time Generation of Delay-Compensated Video Feeds for Outdoor Mobile Robot Teleoperation (ICRA 2025)
cited_work_check.note: Confirmed. It generates 2D delay-compensated images for agricultural robot teleoperation. It is not 3D telepresence.

cited_work_check.title: Evaluating Pose Forecasting for Compensating Network Latency in Full Body Movements (Bohnerth et al., 2025, LNCS)
cited_work_check.note: Title and authors confirmed via Crossref (DFKI, Slusallek). No abstract was available, but the title matches the claim of skeleton/pose forecasting to hide network latency for full-body avatars.

threats.title: GaussianPrediction: Dynamic 3D Gaussian Prediction for Motion Extrapolation and Free View Synthesis
threats.what_overlaps: This is the core technical insight of the cluster. It forecasts future motion of 3D Gaussians (a keypoint GCN plus deformation) and re-renders them to render photoreal future frames from arbitrary viewpoints. It explicitly bridges video prediction and novel view synthesis.
threats.what_remains_different: It is optimised per scene and runs offline. It does not use a live RGB-D or TSDF pipeline, frames nothing as latency compensation, has no uncertainty fallback to a stale frame, no audio, no held-out-camera future supervision for a feed-forward model, and no user study.

threats.title: ODE-GS: Latent ODEs for Dynamic Scene Extrapolation with 3D Gaussian Splatting
threats.what_overlaps: It extrapolates Gaussian trajectories into the future (a transformer plus a latent neural ODE) and renders at arbitrary future timestamps. This is the same idea of 'forecast in 3D on Gaussians, then render'.
threats.what_remains_different: It is per-scene and offline, evaluated on D-NeRF, NVFi and HyperNeRF. It has no real-time streaming, no telepresence latency budget, no stale-versus-forecast hedging, and no audio.

threats.title: Space-Time Forecasting of Dynamic Scenes with Motion-aware Gaussian Grouping (MoGaF)
threats.what_overlaps: It builds on 4DGS with a lightweight forecasting module that predicts future Gaussian motion, rendering future frames that are novel-view capable.
threats.what_remains_different: It targets long-term offline extrapolation of a reconstructed scene. It is not online or feed-forward, not framed around latency, and has no audio.

threats.title: ParticleGS / 4DGS-JEPA / R5DGS (Accelerated Spatio-Temporal Gaussian Rendering via Kinematic and Semantic Priors)
threats.what_overlaps: A growing 2025-2026 body of work on Gaussian dynamics extrapolation and multi-horizon causal prediction over dynamic Gaussians (4DGS-JEPA arXiv 2609.25036; R5DGS arXiv 2605.25909 explicitly motivates forecasting for 'predictive systems').
threats.what_remains_different: All of these are per-scene or physics-driven, focus on objects, and run offline. None works on live captured humans, telepresence latency, or audio.

threats.title: GFFE: G-buffer Free Frame Extrapolation for Low-latency Real-time Rendering (and follow-up Decoupled Motion Prediction for GFFE, ACM MM 2025; Amulet, arXiv 2608.10423)
threats.what_overlaps: The graphics community already treats 'extrapolate future frames, including dynamic-object motion and disocclusion filling, to hide latency' as an established problem, with real-time neural extrapolation of dynamic fragments.
threats.what_remains_different: It works on synthetic game-engine rendered content, not captured multi-view video of people. It uses no multi-view geometry lifting, no novel viewpoints of captured scenes, and no audio.

threats.title: VEST: Forecasting Future Videos from Novel Views via Disentangled 3D Scene Representation
threats.what_overlaps: It shows that lifting to 3D point clouds and forecasting 3D motion beats 2D forecasting for future novel-view frames. That pre-empts the cluster's '3D forecasting is better conditioned than 2D' insight.
threats.what_remains_different: It is monocular, works on driving scenes, runs offline, and has no latency framing, no multi-view rig supervision and no audio.

threats.title: Predictive Display for Teleoperation Based on Vector Fields Using Lidar-Camera Fusion (IJCV 2025 / AAAI 2026 reprint); Predictive Display ... Based on 3D Reconstruction (T-ITS 2025)
threats.what_overlaps: These use 3D geometry (LiDAR) to synthesise latency-compensated future camera images for teleoperation.
threats.what_remains_different: They compensate only ego-vehicle motion and assume a static scene, which is the analogue of ATW. They do not forecast the motion of dynamic content.

threats.title: On the Feasibility of Latency-Controlled Video Transmission Based on Frame Extrapolation (Vijayaratnam, Cagnazzo, Valenzise, Tartaglione)
threats.what_overlaps: It proposes future-frame extrapolation at the receiver to hide transmission latency in video communication. This is the 2D version of the task reformulation.
threats.what_remains_different: It is 2D video only (going by the title; the abstract was inaccessible). It has no 3D, no free viewpoint and no audio conditioning.

threats.title: Real-Time Interactions Between Human Controllers and Remote Devices in Metaverse
threats.what_overlaps: It predicts human motion with an adaptive prediction horizon for proactive rendering to cut motion-to-photon latency. This echoes the 'adaptive horizon' idea.
threats.what_remains_different: It works on controller or skeleton motion driving virtual models, not photoreal captured 3D video, and has no audio.

threats.title: DyStream: Streaming Dyadic Talking Heads Generation (and Personalizing Causal Audio-Driven Facial Motion, arXiv 2604.23692)
threats.what_overlaps: It does real-time audio-driven face and mouth synthesis under latency budgets, with an explicit 60 ms audio lookahead trade-off. 2604.23692 targets causal, zero-lookahead audio-driven facial motion for telepresence.
threats.what_remains_different: Both generate avatars or talking heads from audio. Neither uses audio arriving ahead of video to forecast mouth motion in captured multi-view 3D video while keeping real pixels.

novelty.remaining_novel_angle:
I found no work, in any community, that uses causal forecasting to hide the glass-to-glass latency of live, captured multi-view RGB-D 3D video of people. The defensible package has five parts:

1. The task and protocol: evaluate free-viewpoint telepresence against ground truth at display time t+Δ at held-out rig cameras, and report latency-versus-quality curves showing that time-aligned evaluation changes method rankings.
2. A feed-forward, real-time forecaster. It advects per-view pixel-Gaussians along TSDF-lifted scene flow and keeps observed appearance. It is trained with future held-out-camera frames as free supervision, unlike the offline per-scene optimisation in GaussianPrediction, ODE-GS, MoGaF and ParticleGS.
3. Hedging between the forecast and the stale frame under uncertainty, with an analysis of the optimal horizon.
4. Exploiting the fact that audio packets arrive before the volumetric video, so the mouth region of real captured 3D video is conditioned on audio that has already arrived. Existing audio-driven work either synthesises avatars or treats audio lookahead as a latency cost.
5. An HMD user study on interaction timing.

The claim that 3D forecasting on Gaussians, followed by re-splatting, handles parallax and occlusion better than 2D is not novel. GaussianPrediction, ODE-GS and VEST already establish it, and GFFE-style frame extrapolation already frames generating future frames as latency hiding. The paper should therefore present its 3D-versus-2D gains as supporting evidence, not as the contribution.
novelty.best_variant:
The strongest combination is Idea 1's reformulation and benchmark plus Idea 2's audio-asymmetry mouth conditioning.

Idea 1's parts: time-aligned t+Δ evaluation at held-out rig cameras, latency-quality curves, and uncertainty hedging toward the stale frame. Its '3D beats 2D forecasting' claim has already been shown by GaussianPrediction (SIGGRAPH 2024), ODE-GS (ICLR 2026) and VEST (ECCV 2024), so it cannot carry novelty.

Idea 2's audio-asymmetry mouth conditioning is the most distinctive technical element with no prior hit. DyStream and 2604.23692 treat audio lookahead only as a cost in avatar synthesis.

The benchmark reformulation plus a real-time feed-forward, appearance-preserving forecaster built into the base pipeline is the part that is hardest to scoop. The audio branch should be a clearly separable second contribution, because it needs audio-visual multi-view data that may require new capture. Reviewers will compare against GaussianPrediction, ODE-GS and GFFE, so those must be baselines or discussed explicitly.

sharpened.title: Rendering the Present: Latency-Aware Evaluation and No-Regret, Audio-Led Forecasting for Live Free-Viewpoint Telepresence
sharpened.one_liner: Evaluate online 3D video against what the remote scene looks like when the frame is displayed, not when it was captured. Close part of that gap with a feed-forward causal forecaster that moves real captured RGB-D pixel-Gaussians forward in time, is guaranteed not to do worse than the stale frame, and uses speech audio that has already arrived to drive the mouth.
sharpened.core_claim: The claim holds on public multi-view human video (DyNeRF, DNA-Rendering, MVHumanNet++) at held-out rig cameras. With an end-to-end latency of Δ = 100-167 ms, a feed-forward, geometry-grounded forecaster with a no-regret hedge must meet three conditions. (a) It recovers at least 40% of the dynamic-region perceptual gap between the stale render and an oracle future render. The metrics are motion-masked LPIPS and 2D hand/body keypoint error at t+Δ. (b) It is never worse than the stale reprojection by more than 0.5% LPIPS on any test sequence. (c) It adds at most 10 ms per frame on a single consumer GPU. A second claim concerns audio. When audio plays immediately (not delayed for lip sync), the audio-led mouth forecast should cut lip-sync error (LSE-D) at the display time by at least 50% compared with a stale mouth. In an HMD study, participants should rate audio-visual asynchrony no worse than with audio held back for lip sync. The claim is falsified if either the gap recovery or the no-regret bound fails at Δ = 100 ms, or if the audio-led mouth does not beat the stale mouth on LSE-D and on asynchrony ratings.
sharpened.key_insight:
1. Time-aligned evaluation. Glass-to-glass latency makes every online NVS method render the past, and a calibrated rig provides exact, free supervision for the present: score the held-out camera at t+Δ. Once each method's measured latency sets its Δ, the latency-quality trade-off becomes a first-class object of analysis, and rankings between slow-but-accurate and fast methods can flip. This is new to the NVS and telepresence literature.

2. No-regret forecasting. Image-based telepresence must look authentic, so the forecaster should move observed pixels rather than generate them. It advects the base pipeline's per-view pixel-Gaussians using TSDF-grounded 3D scene flow and triangulated 3D keypoint trajectories, and the rig's difference masks mean static pixels need no forecast at all. A learned hedge falls back to the stale reprojection whenever the forecast is uncertain. The target is therefore not 'predict the future' but 'never be worse than showing the past, and be better where motion is predictable'.

3. Audio arrives first. A 3D video pipeline adds capture, depth, fusion and encoding delay that audio does not have, so audio for times up to roughly t+Δ_a is already at the receiver when frame t is rendered. The mouth at display time is then conditioned on audio that has already arrived, which is well-posed audio-to-motion synthesis rather than guesswork. Receivers can stop delaying audio for lip sync, which removes delay from the conversational path.
sharpened.method:
Base: the Ha et al. pipeline, or an equivalent re-implementation. It forward-splats per-view pixel-Gaussians, runs a colour-gated temporal depth filter, performs image-space TSDF ray-marching and applies the 4-level U-Net blender.

1. State (history of k = 4 frames). Per-view filtered depth and TSDF-rendered depth, difference masks, RGB, and fast optical flow (NeuFlow/RAFT-small at 1/4 resolution) between t-1 and t. The flow and depth are lifted to per-pixel 3D scene flow. 2D body, hand and face keypoints come from a streaming RTMPose-class detector and are triangulated with the known calibration into 3D keypoint tracks.

2. Forecaster, which operates only on pixels inside the dynamic mask:
   - (a) A small causal transformer on the 3D keypoint tracks predicts keypoint positions at Δ ∈ {33..233} ms. It outputs Laplace uncertainty and is Δ-conditioned via FiLM.
   - (b) Keypoint motion is transferred to Gaussians by learned soft skinning weights, i.e. nearest-keypoint weights refined by a network, with no parametric body model.
   - (c) A per-view ConvGRU at 1/4 resolution predicts a residual 3D displacement and a per-pixel log-variance. This covers clothing, hair and objects in hand.

3. Audio branch. A causal distilled HuBERT/wav2vec encoder reads audio up to t+Δ_a, where Δ_a is the measured audio lead at runtime. It cross-attends to mouth-region Gaussians, which are selected by face keypoints. It predicts lip and jaw 3D displacement plus a small inner-mouth appearance residual, output through the blender's background/residual head. The mouth is the only place where appearance is synthesised.

4. Rendering. Advected Gaussians are splatted to the viewer pose predicted for t+Δ, using a standard Kalman head predictor. The TSDF is ray-marched on the advected depths.

5. No-regret hedge. The blend U-Net receives extra channels: the stale reprojection (the stale content rendered at the new pose, i.e. an ATW baseline), the uncertainty map and Δ. It outputs a per-pixel gate α. The final image is the α-weighted combination of the forecast render and the stale reprojection.

Losses:
- L1 + SSIM + LPIPS at the held-out camera at t+Δ, weighted up in motion regions.
- Depth L1 against the future TSDF depth.
- Laplace NLL on the 3D keypoints.
- A no-regret hinge: max(0, LPIPS_patch(out) - LPIPS_patch(stale) + m).
- A temporal warping loss.
- For the mouth, a SyncNet-feature lip-sync loss plus L1.

Training. A curriculum over Δ on DyNeRF/N3DV, DNA-Rendering and MVHumanNet++, with test subjects held out as well as test cameras. The audio branch is pretrained on Multiface speech sequences (multi-view, 30 fps, with audio) and fine-tuned on a small in-house capture.

Runtime budget on an RTX 4090 at 640x352, K = 4: keypoints 3 ms, flow 3 ms, forecaster plus skinning 3 ms, audio 2 ms, for a total of ≤ 10 ms over the base pipeline.

An adaptive horizon falls out of the hedge: the effective lead time is where α drops below 0.5.
sharpened.why_not_engineering:
There are three scientific contributions, not a speed-up.

1. A new evaluation principle. Free-viewpoint video quality should be measured at display time. The paper shows empirically that this changes conclusions: the ranking of online NVS methods changes once measured latency is charged, and the frame-rate-versus-quality optimum moves.

2. A characterisation of human-motion predictability for photoreal free-viewpoint video. This includes latency-quality curves, the headroom between the stale render and the oracle as a function of Δ and body part, and where 3D grounding helps over 2D. It comes with a forecaster that carries an explicit no-regret guarantee, trained with an objective that makes 'never worse than stale' measurable and testable.

3. A new observation about the latency structure of 3D telepresence: audio leads volumetric video. It turns lip-sync from 'delay audio' into 'let video catch up', and the paper validates this perceptually in an HMD study.

Each of these can be falsified independently. None is an implementation detail of the base pipeline.
sharpened.differentiation:
GaussianPrediction (SIGGRAPH 2024, https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.19745), ODE-GS (ICLR 2026, https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.05480), MoGaF (https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.21668) and ParticleGS (https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.20270) extrapolate Gaussian dynamics after per-scene optimisation, offline, and without latency framing. This paper does not claim that 3D forecasting beats 2D. That is treated as supporting evidence, and these methods are run as per-scene causal-window baselines where feasible. What this paper adds is a feed-forward, cross-subject, real-time forecaster with a no-regret hedge, plus the time-aligned protocol.

VEST (ECCV 2024, https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.21450) already showed that 3D-lifted forecasting helps, but for offline monocular driving scenes. It is cited as the reason the 3D-versus-2D claim is not a contribution here.

GFFE (https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.18551) and its follow-ups perform latency-hiding frame extrapolation for synthetic, game-engine-rendered content with G-buffers. This paper targets captured multi-view humans, novel viewpoints and audio. A GFFE-style 2D extrapolator is run on the rendered output as a baseline.

Predictive-display work (https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.09670, https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.09921, https://doi.org/10.1007/s11263-025-02550-z) forecasts in 2D or compensates only ego-motion. Streaming 3DGS for latency (https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.02851) compensates viewpoint latency, not motion of the content. NoPo4D (https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.22190) uses velocities only for interpolation within the observed time window.

Audio-driven telepresence faces (https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.01176) and DyStream (https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.24408) synthesise avatars and treat audio lookahead as a latency cost. This paper keeps real captured pixels and exploits audio lookahead that already exists.

Avatar pose forecasting (https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-032-03805-0_3) and Mon3tr (https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.07518) work on parametric avatars, not image-based, authentic 3D video.

datasets: DyNeRF / Neural 3D Video (public, about 18-21 cameras, 30 fps). The cooking and hand-motion scenes are the base paper's own benchmark and give direct comparability.
DNA-Rendering (public on application, many cameras). Diverse human motion and objects in hand; the frame rate is lower (verify), which is acceptable for Δ at multiples of one frame.
MVHumanNet++ (public on application, large-scale multi-view humans). Used for cross-subject training and a held-out-subject test.
ENeRF-Outdoor (public). A robustness check on outdoor multi-person scenes.
CMU Panoptic Studio. The social and haggling sequences give conversational body motion; check which sequences include usable audio and HD sync.

Multiface (public, https://github.com/facebookresearch/multiface): multi-view faces (about 40-160 views, 30 fps) with audio. Used to pretrain and evaluate the audio-led mouth branch; missing frames must be handled when aligning audio.

NeRSemble (https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.03027: 16 cameras, 73 fps, includes speech). The high frame rate allows fine-grained Δ for the face; whether audio is released is unconfirmed, so verify before relying on it.

Custom capture (needed): a small rig of 8-12 synced RGB cameras plus 2-4 RGB-D cameras, with a genlocked microphone. 10-20 participants in upper-body conversation, gesturing and handing over objects. Required for the joint body+audio evaluation and the HMD user study.
baselines: Stale render: the base pipeline showing frame t at time t+Δ (the status quo).
Stale reprojection: the stale content re-rendered at the viewer pose for t+Δ using TSDF depth (the ATW/late-latching analogue).
2D extrapolation on the rendered output: constant-velocity optical-flow warp, plus a GFFE-style learned 2D extrapolator retrained on the same data.
Distilled causal 2D video predictor on the rendered output, the model family from 2605.09670, as a representative of generative predictive display.
Constant-velocity 3D advection of pixel-Gaussians (the NoPo4D-velocity analogue, with no learning).
Per-scene Gaussian forecasters, GaussianPrediction and ODE-GS, fitted on a causal window, to show the accuracy/runtime/generalisation trade-off.
Skeleton forecasting plus LBS warp without a residual (the avatar pose-forecasting analogue).
Oracle: the base pipeline run on true future inputs (upper bound).
Audio: stale mouth; delayed-audio lip sync (the status quo); an off-the-shelf 2D lip-sync editor applied independently per view (tests multi-view consistency).
metrics: Time-aligned PSNR, SSIM and LPIPS at held-out cameras at t+Δ, full-frame and motion-masked, plotted as latency-quality curves over Δ ∈ {33..233} ms.
Headroom recovered = (Q_forecast - Q_stale) / (Q_oracle - Q_stale), per Δ and per body part.
2D hand/body keypoint error at t+Δ, from a detector run on the render and on ground truth.
Worst-case regret: the maximum over sequences and patches of (LPIPS_out - LPIPS_stale). Also a false-motion rate: the fraction of frames with a predicted gesture onset where ground truth has none.
Temporal consistency (TCC/STED or a warping error) and flicker.
Lip sync: LSE-D and LSE-C at display time; mouth-landmark error.
Cross-view consistency of the forecast (e.g. MEt3R or epipolar consistency).
Added runtime (ms) and memory on a stated GPU; measured glass-to-glass latency of the rig system.

User study (HMD, emulated delay of 0/100/200/300 ms): hand-clap and handover synchrony error, turn-taking gap and overlap, audio-visual asynchrony ratings, perceived lag (JND via staircase), artifact and naturalness ratings, co-presence questionnaire.
Latency-aware ranking of existing online NVS methods (the base paper, GPS-Gaussian, ENeRF-class methods), each charged its measured latency.
key_ablations: 3D (TSDF-lifted) versus 2D forecasting, evaluated at novel views.
Keypoint-skinning prior versus a dense-flow-only forecaster versus both.
No-regret hinge and gate on or off: effect on mean quality and on worst-case regret.
Δ-conditioning versus separate per-Δ models; fixed versus adaptive horizon.
Audio-led mouth versus a video-only mouth forecast versus a stale mouth, sweeping the audio lead Δ_a ∈ {0, 50, 100, 150} ms.
History length k and the resolution of the forecaster.
Using the rig difference mask to skip static pixels: runtime and quality.
Training data: DyNeRF only versus adding DNA-Rendering and MVHumanNet++, tested on held-out subjects.
experiments.capture_notes:
The core forecasting claims (C1, the no-regret claim and the time-aligned protocol) can be tested entirely on public data: DyNeRF, DNA-Rendering, MVHumanNet++ and Panoptic. The audio branch can be pretrained and evaluated at face level on Multiface (multi-view with audio, confirmed on the GitHub page). NeRSemble's audio availability must be verified.

A custom capture is needed for three things: joint full/upper-body plus audio conversational data, measuring the real audio-versus-3D-video latency asymmetry in a working pipeline, and the HMD user study. A small rig is enough: 8-12 genlocked machine-vision cameras plus 2-4 RGB-D cameras (e.g. Azure Kinect or Orbbec) and a synced microphone, about 15-30k USD. That is 2-4 weeks of capture with 10-20 consenting participants, and IRB approval is required for both the capture and the study. Release the captured set (with consent) as a latency-aware telepresence benchmark to strengthen the paper.

review.kill_criteria:
Kill or pivot if any of the following holds.

1. The headroom at Δ = 100 ms is negligible on dynamic regions of public human data: motion-masked LPIPS gap below about 0.02 and keypoint error below about 5 px at 640 px. Latency would then be invisible to metrics, and the paper would rest entirely on a user study; pivot to a pure IEEE VR/CHI perception study.

2. After about 6 weeks of learning, the forecaster recovers less than 35% of the headroom at Δ = 100 ms on held-out subjects.

3. The forecaster cannot meet the no-regret bound, i.e. it is worse than stale reprojection on more than 10% of sequences, without collapsing to the stale frame everywhere (α ≈ 0).

4. 3D forecasting shows no advantage over 2D flow extrapolation at held-out views. That removes the geometry-grounded story; the protocol could still be salvaged as a benchmark or workshop paper.

5. The measured audio lead Δ_a in a realistic pipeline is below about 40 ms, or the audio-led mouth does not reduce LSE-D by at least 30% compared with a stale mouth. In that case drop the audio branch and keep the body forecaster.

6. A pilot perception test (N ≈ 8, 150 ms injected delay) shows that participants prefer stale-but-real over forecast, or cannot tell the difference in synchrony tasks.

reviewer_objections.objection: This is GaussianPrediction, ODE-GS or VEST (3D forecasting on Gaussians or points, then re-render) bolted onto an IBR pipeline. The 3D-beats-2D insight is known.
Human motion beyond about 100 ms is largely unpredictable, so the forecaster will either hallucinate gestures, which harms authenticity, or regress to the stale frame, which gives no gain.
reviewer_objections.rebuttal: The paper quantifies exactly this with latency-quality curves broken down by body part. The hedge makes the system degrade to the status quo rather than below it, and the worst-case regret and false-motion rates are reported. Even partial compensation, such as 50-80 ms of arm and hand motion or the audio-grounded mouth, is perceptually meaningful. The HMD study measures whether net perceived benefit is positive. Only motion is forecast; pixels stay real.

reviewer_objections.objection: PSNR or LPIPS at t+Δ rewards blur, and the stale frame is a very strong baseline because most pixels are static. The gains are either tiny or metric artifacts.
reviewer_objections.rebuttal: The primary metrics are motion-masked perceptual error, keypoint error at t+Δ, and the fraction of the stale-to-oracle headroom recovered, not full-frame PSNR. Sharpness and temporal metrics penalise blur, and the user study measures interaction timing directly. An oracle upper bound is always reported, so the size of the gap is transparent.

reviewer_objections.objection: 'Audio arrives before video' is an artifact of your system. RTC stacks synchronise the streams in the jitter buffer, and ultra-low-latency 3D pipelines would remove the asymmetry.
reviewer_objections.rebuttal: The asymmetry is structural: volumetric video needs capture, depth estimation, fusion, encoding and view-dependent rendering, which audio does not. The paper measures it stage by stage in a working pipeline and reports results as a function of Δ_a, including 0. Today receivers pay for the asymmetry by delaying audio to keep lip sync. The contribution reverses that trade-off, and the user study tests audio held back against audio-immediate with the forecast mouth.

reviewer_objections.objection: Showing synthetic, forecast frames in telepresence is ethically problematic (fabricated expressions), and the evaluation on 30 fps offline datasets is far from a real deployed call.
reviewer_objections.rebuttal: Appearance is synthesised only in the mouth interior. Everything else is real captured pixels, moved by at most Δ ≤ 233 ms, and the gate falls back to real content under uncertainty. The system can expose a confidence or provenance flag, linking to trust and provenance directions. The paper includes a live rig demo with emulated network delay and measured glass-to-glass latency, not only offline datasets.

effort.months: 8-10: 2 for the probe and protocol, 3-4 for the forecaster, 2 for the audio branch and capture, 2 for the user study and writing
effort.people: 2 (one PhD student on the forecaster and protocol; one on the rig, audio branch and user study), plus an advisor with HCI/perception experience for the study design
effort.compute: 2-4 GPUs (A100 or RTX 4090 class). The forecaster is small; most compute goes to running the base pipeline and oracle renders across datasets. A small rig of 8-12 RGB plus 2-4 RGB-D cameras and a mic (about 15-30k USD) or a borrowed capture lab; an HMD (Quest 3 or Vision Pro class) for the study.

review.venue: SIGGRAPH Asia 2027 (ACM TOG), a method plus user study; the fallback is ISMAR 2027 or IEEE VR 2028 (TVCG). If the headroom probe is strong but the user study slips, a CVPR 2027 or 3DV submission of the protocol plus forecaster is possible, with the user study held for a TVCG extension.
review.synergies:
Latency-aware benchmark (landscape gap on unified telepresence benchmarks): the time-aligned t+Δ protocol and captured audio-visual rig data become one track of a larger telepresence benchmark (fidelity, temporal and stereo consistency, latency).

TSDF-based late reprojection / ASW for remote content: the same forecaster at Δ below one capture interval upsamples 30 fps captured content to 72-90 Hz HMD refresh, and it shares the stale-reprojection baseline. This could be a joint paper or a series.

Packet-loss and frame-drop concealment, and bandwidth-aware receiver synthesis: forecasting at the receiver hides dropped or late frames.

Streaming geometry foundation models (StreamVGGT and similar): these could supply the scene flow and depth history more cheaply.

Compute-split and cloud rendering: forecasting makes cloud rendering with 150-300 ms round trips usable.

Provenance and trust labelling of synthetic content: the forecast-confidence map doubles as a provenance signal.

Audio-driven codec avatars: the audio-lead principle transfers to hybrid IBR-avatar systems such as Mon3tr.

name: Latency-hiding split rendering with layered RGB-D view bundles for standalone headsets

cited_work_check.title: Streaming Real-Time Rendered Scenes as 3D Gaussians (Siekkinen & Kamarainen)
cited_work_check.note: Submitted 3 Apr 2026. The server builds and incrementally updates a live 3DGS from real-time rendered reference views of synthetic Unity scenes. It streams snapshots and deltas so clients can compensate latency, and compares against conventional image warping. The ideator describes it correctly: synthetic content, not captured people. It does occupy the 'ship a 3D representation for client-side latency compensation' framing.

cited_work_check.title: CAGS: Color-Adaptive Volumetric Video Streaming with Dynamic 3D Gaussian Splatting
cited_work_check.note: SIGGRAPH 2026, submitted 10 May 2026. VQ-based LODs, with server-rendered low-res reference images used to restore colour under bandwidth constraints. It targets bandwidth adaptation, not latency hiding, as the ideator says.

cited_work_check.title: Low-latency Cloud-based Volumetric Video Streaming Using Head Motion Prediction (Gul et al.)
cited_work_check.note: Renders 2D views of pre-recorded volumetric video in the cloud from predicted head pose. Accurate. The same group also published image warping for latency compensation (ICIP 2022, https://doi.org/10.1109/icip46576.2022.9897163), which the ideator did not cite. That paper uses homography late-warp plus prediction.

cited_work_check.title: Kalman Filter-based Head Motion Prediction for Cloud-based Mixed Reality
cited_work_check.note: Kalman head-pose prediction for cloud rendering of volumetric video, compared against an autoregression model at 60 ms look-ahead. Accurate.

cited_work_check.title: Mon3tr: Monocular 3D Telepresence with Pre-built Gaussian Avatars as Amortization
cited_work_check.note: Exists (Jan 2026) and runs on Quest 3 with a parametric Gaussian avatar. The abstract gives about 80 ms end-to-end, not 73 ms (73 ms may be a component figure in the body). This is a minor numeric discrepancy; the characterisation is otherwise correct.

cited_work_check.title: Project Starline
cited_work_check.note: Not re-opened. Well known: receiver-side rendering on a desktop-class GPU with an autostereo display. The claim is accurate.

threats.title: QuadStream: A Quad-Based Scene Streaming Architecture for Novel Viewpoint Reconstruction (Hladky et al.)
threats.what_overlaps: The core systems insight. The server streams a disocclusion-robust, layered or approximate-geometry representation covering a view cell of possible client poses. A thin VR/phone client then reconstructs and renders the current and nearby views, cutting motion-to-photon latency without the disocclusion holes of video-plus-reprojection. 'Size the extra layers or coverage by the pose range' is exactly the view-cell or potentially-visible-set (PVS) idea, and the lineage runs back to Camera Offset Space and Shading Atlas Streaming.
threats.what_remains_different: Built for synthetic scenes with a full G-buffer and known hidden geometry. It does not use live multi-camera capture, noisy estimated depth or IBR shading of occluded layers, and it does not treat temporal shimmer from per-frame depth noise.

threats.title: Potentially Visible Set Generation with the Disocclusion Buffer (Kunzel et al.)
threats.what_overlaps: From-region PVS computed on a sparse, layered, depth-quantised scene representation. It lists streaming rendering and framerate upsampling as target uses and directly computes what becomes disoccluded over a range of camera motion. This is the 'which hidden layers to send for the predicted pose region' step.
threats.what_remains_different: Synthetic rendering only. It includes no captured data, pose-uncertainty-driven sizing, network system or telepresence evaluation.

threats.title: Potentially Visible Hidden-Volume Rendering for Multi-View Warping (Kim & Lee)
threats.what_overlaps: Depth-peeled hidden layers restricted to fragments that are occluded at the source view but may be visible within a bound of novel views, used for multi-view warping. This is essentially 'layer count and extent sized by the view bound', with multi-layer extraction feeding warping.
threats.what_remains_different: No streaming or network latency, synthetic geometry, and no uncertainty-derived bound or live capture.

threats.title: MeshReduce: Split Rendering of Live 3D Scene for Virtual Teleportation / MeshReduce: Scalable and Bandwidth Efficient 3D Scene Capture (Jin, Lu, Dasari, ... Rowe, CMU)
threats.what_overlaps: Live multi-depth-sensor capture of people and scene, streamed through a split-rendering framework to mobile AR/VR and browsers for telepresence. It directly occupies 'split rendering of live 3D capture for teleportation on light clients'.
threats.what_remains_different: Streams textured meshes and renders them on the client. There is no layered RGB-D bundle from a learned IBR pipeline, no pose-uncertainty-sized guard band or layers, and no study of reprojection shimmer or display-rate temporal consistency.

threats.title: Towards Interactive Volumetric Video experiences on Lightweight VR Devices through Remote Rendering (Fernandez-Dasi et al.)
threats.what_overlaps: End-to-end remote rendering of VR scenes containing live volumetric video feeds of holoported users to standalone headsets and browsers. It uses viewport-aware stereoscopic projections with margin beyond the field of view and reports motion-to-photon latency (under 40 ms local, about 180 ms over the Internet).
threats.what_remains_different: Video-projection delivery with no layered depth or late depth reprojection. The source is conventional volumetric video, not geometry-guided IBR, and no temporal-consistency analysis is reported.

threats.title: Latency Compensation Through Image Warping For Remote Rendering-Based Volumetric Video Streaming (Gul, Hellge, Eisert)
threats.what_overlaps: Server rendering of volumetric humans from predicted pose, plus client late-warp at the latest pose. This is the same predict-then-render-then-late-warp loop, applied to volumetric people.
threats.what_remains_different: Planar homography only: no depth, no layers, no disocclusion handling, and pre-recorded content.

threats.title: CollabVR: Reprojection-Based Edge-Client Collaborative Rendering for Mobile VR (Ke et al.)
threats.what_overlaps: The edge renders one RGB-D view and the HMD reprojects it with depth-image-based rendering (DIBR) under a real-time mobile GPU budget, including foveated patch-subdivided warping. This is the client-side reprojector design.
threats.what_remains_different: Reprojection covers the second eye, not latency hiding, and the content is synthetic with single-layer depth.

threats.title: EdgeGaussian: Real-time Free-Viewpoint Video for Mobile VR via Edge-Client Collaborative Neural Rendering (Ke et al.)
threats.what_overlaps: Edge-client split of free-viewpoint video (FVV) rendering for untethered HMDs. The static scene is a local mesh and the dynamic 4DGS runs on the edge, reaching up to 128 FPS, with telepresence as a stated application.
threats.what_remains_different: Offline-reconstructed 4DGS, with a static/dynamic split rather than latency-hiding layered bundles. Not geometry-guided IBR of live capture.

threats.title: Streaming Real-Time Rendered Scenes as 3D Gaussians
threats.what_overlaps: Argues for streaming a 3D representation instead of 2D video so clients can compensate latency better than image warping. This is the same motivation and would be a natural baseline.
threats.what_remains_different: Synthetic Unity scenes, a full 3DGS rather than a compact layered RGB-D bundle, and no live people.

threats.title: Vues: practical mobile volumetric video streaming through multiview transcoding (Liu et al.)
threats.what_overlaps: The edge transcodes volumetric frames into multiple 2D views for predicted viewports, trading extra views against QoE. This is the hedge-against-pose-prediction-error idea in a networking venue.
threats.what_remains_different: Multiple flat views with no depth layers or reprojection, and pre-recorded point clouds.

threats.title: MPEG Immersive Video (MIV) texture+depth atlas coding
threats.venue: Immersive Video Technologies (book chapter), MPEG-I standard
threats.what_overlaps: HEVC-coded atlases of texture and depth patches, including occluded content, for client-side 6DoF view synthesis. The proposed 'tiled video atlas with 10-bit depth' codec is essentially MIV.
threats.what_remains_different: Transmits source views and patches rather than a server-rendered, pose-predicted layered bundle. Not tied to a latency-hiding loop.

novelty.remaining_novel_angle:
The systems skeleton is well-trodden prior art: predict pose, render on server or edge, ship a disocclusion-robust layered or PVS representation sized to a view region, then late-reproject on the thin client. See QuadStream 2022, Kim & Lee PVHV 2023, the SIGGRAPH Asia 2025 Disocclusion Buffer, Gul et al. 2020-22, Vues, and CollabVR. The atlas codec is essentially MPEG Immersive Video (MIV). Split rendering of live multi-depth-sensor telepresence also exists (MeshReduce, IEEE VR 2024; the IMX 2026 remote-rendering work with holoported users). None of these components is new on its own.

What survives:
(1) Captured-data layered bundles. Occluded layers come from multi-hit raymarching of a live, temporally filtered TSDF and are shaded by a learned multi-view IBR blend net from the rig cameras that actually observed those surfaces. Prior PVS and layered streaming assumes synthetic scenes with an exact G-buffer.
(2) Temporal consistency as a first-class requirement of late reprojection. Neither the synthetic-scene streaming literature nor the live-capture systems measure or optimise shimmer. The claim to test is that depth consistency across frames and views is what makes depth-based reprojection of live humans shimmer-free; that requires a display-rate (90 Hz) flicker metric on the reprojected output.
(3) End-to-end training of the IBR blend or shading network with losses on reprojected outputs at sampled true poses (reprojection-aware training). No surveyed work does this for captured content.
(4) Sizing guard band and layer count from the covariance of a probabilistic pose predictor. This is a modest step beyond fixed view cells and is the weakest of the four claims.

The paper should be pitched as the 'captured-content, temporally-consistent' counterpart of QuadStream/PVS streaming, not as a new split-rendering architecture. It must cite and beat QuadStream-style and MeshReduce-style baselines, plus single-layer DIBR with raw depth.
novelty.best_variant: The cluster holds only one idea ("Predict, Bundle, Reproject"). Its most defensible sub-claim is the combination of contributions 2 and 4: temporally consistent geometry-guided depth is the enabler of shimmer-free late reprojection of live people, and the blend net is trained and evaluated with a display-rate (90 Hz) temporal-consistency loss and metric on the reprojected stream. That half has no direct precedent in the PVS/QuadStream line (synthetic, no noise) or in live-capture split rendering (MeshReduce, IMX 2026, Gul et al.), none of which study reprojection shimmer. The multi-hit TSDF layer extraction with IBR shading of occluded layers is a secondary but real novelty, because captured rigs actually observe the hidden surfaces. The uncertainty-sized guard band, layered atlas codec and client reprojector are engineering on top of QuadStream, PVHV, Disocclusion Buffer and MIV prior art. Claim them as system contributions, not research novelty.

sharpened.title: Render for the Display, Not the Frame: Reprojection-Stable Geometry-Guided View Synthesis for Latency-Hidden Telepresence on Standalone Headsets
sharpened.one_liner: Live multi-view IBR is trained and evaluated on the frames the headset actually shows after late reprojection under real pose-prediction error. This shows that cross-time and cross-view depth consistency, which barely registers when images are rendered directly, largely determines shimmer and hole artefacts once split rendering hides network latency.
sharpened.core_claim: We make one falsifiable claim. For live-captured people rendered on an edge server at a predicted pose and late-reprojected on a standalone HMD, temporally consistent, multi-view-fused depth (TSDF with temporal filtering) cuts display-rate flicker substantially (target at least 30% lower warping error or FovVideoVDP-temporal gain) and lowers LPIPS against ground truth at the true pose. The effect holds relative to per-frame stereo or MVS depth of equal single-frame accuracy. The gap grows with prediction horizon (RTT + render time, 20 to 150 ms), while the same depth change is nearly invisible (below 0.1 dB, as in the base paper's ablation) when frames are rendered directly at the true pose. A second claim is that training the blend or shading network with a loss on reprojected outputs at sampled pose errors beats training at the rendered pose. The 2-layer IBR-shaded bundle is expected to beat a wider-FoV single layer at equal bitrate only beyond a translation-error threshold, which we measure.
sharpened.key_insight: Late reprojection turns depth error into image motion. Warp displacement is roughly f·|Δt_pose|·δz/z². Frame-to-frame depth noise therefore becomes display-rate shimmer, amplified in proportion to pose-prediction error. Per-frame metrics at the rendered pose cannot see this, which explains why the base paper's TSDF ablation looks like a no-op. Captured rigs actually observe surfaces hidden from the predicted viewpoint, so unlike PVS/QuadStream streaming of synthetic G-buffers, occluded layers can be both extracted (multi-hit TSDF raymarch) and photometrically shaded from real cameras. The right optimisation target is the reprojected, displayed 90 Hz stream, integrated over the pose-error distribution.
sharpened.method: Server (edge GPU, 30 Hz budget of 33 ms or less, 2x ~1K per-eye bundle): (a) the base geometry-guided pipeline, or an open reimplementation (forward-splatted per-view depth, temporal filter, image-based TSDF). The previous-frame depth feedback is redefined in a fixed world or rig frame and explicitly reprojected, which fixes the base paper's moving-target gap. (b) Multi-hit TSDF raymarching yields L≤2 layers: the first surface, then the next surface past a depth discontinuity, extracted only inside a disocclusion guard region. (c) The blend net is extended with a layer index and per-source visibility (depth test of each rig camera against the layer), so hidden layers are shaded from the cameras that saw them, with an alpha/edge band. (d) A pose predictor (Kalman filter or a small GRU with heteroscedastic output) predicts over RTT+render. Its covariance sets guard-band width and whether to emit layer 2. This part is a system component, not a claimed novelty. Transport: tiled HEVC 10-bit texture+depth atlas, MIV-like, reused and not claimed. Client (Quest 3, OpenXR/Vulkan compute, 3 ms or less for both eyes): per-vsync layered forward warp with front-to-back compositing, stereo from one bundle plus IPD shift, and a cheap hole fill. Training: pose errors Δ are sampled from residuals of the predictor on recorded HMD head traces. On dense public rigs the true pose p is a held-out camera and the predicted pose is p̂ = p − Δ. The bundle is rendered at p̂ and warped to p. Losses: L1+LPIPS versus GT at p; a display-rate temporal loss (occlusion-masked flow-warping error between consecutive warped outputs for a fixed true pose while p̂ and capture time vary); and a depth temporal-consistency regulariser in world space. Training data: ActorsHQ and DNA-Rendering (dense human rigs), plus DyNeRF and ENeRF-Outdoor for scenes.
sharpened.why_not_engineering: The contribution is a measured phenomenon, a method change and a metric, not a pipeline. (1) A quantitative law, validated empirically, links depth temporal noise and pose-prediction horizon to displayed flicker for captured content. It explains why depth consistency looks useless under standard NVS evaluation but dominates under reprojection. (2) Reprojection-aware training changes what the IBR network learns. It should reduce reliance on unstable depth at silhouettes, and we test this with an ablation. (3) An evaluation protocol for latency-hidden telepresence, reprojected ground truth on dense rigs at display rate with FovVideoVDP-style temporal scoring, which no existing live-capture NVS paper uses. The codec, predictor and client warper are explicitly framed as enabling system work.
sharpened.differentiation: Versus QuadStream (TOG 2022), PVHV (Kim & Lee, TOG 2023) and the Disocclusion Buffer PVS (SIGGRAPH Asia 2025): those assume synthetic scenes with an exact G-buffer and noiseless depth, so shimmer from depth noise does not exist for them, and hidden layers are rasterised rather than estimated and IBR-shaded from real cameras. We inherit their view-cell idea and cite it as such. Versus MeshReduce (IEEE VR 2024), the IMX 2026 volumetric remote rendering work and MetaStream: they deliver live capture to light clients as meshes, point clouds or flat projections and do not study reprojection shimmer or train for it. Versus Gul et al. (2020-22 cloud volumetric plus Kalman prediction plus homography late-warp): theirs is pre-recorded content with planar warping and no depth layers. Versus CPSL (arXiv 2511.14927): offline 2.5D layered volumetric video for playback, with no pose-predicted live bundle and no latency loop. Versus Streaming-3DGS (arXiv 2604.02851), EdgeGaussian (MobiCom 2025) and CAGS (SIGGRAPH 2026): these ship full 3D representations of synthetic or offline content and serve as Pareto baselines (bitrate, client ms) rather than conflicting claims. Versus the base paper (Ha et al., CVPR 2025): it never measures head-tracked or display-rate output, has no temporal loss, and leaves feedback reprojection for a moving target undefined.
