experiments.capture_notes: The core scientific claim (depth consistency x prediction horizon -> displayed flicker; reprojection-aware training) can be tested entirely on public dense multi-view datasets (ActorsHQ, DNA-Rendering, Panoptic, DyNeRF) with an emulated latency loop. The true pose is a held-out camera, the predicted pose is offset by residuals from real HMD head traces, and ground truth exists only at capture rate. Display-rate flicker is therefore measured with GT-free warping-error and VDP metrics, plus GT comparison at capture instants. Custom work is only needed for (a) recording head-pose traces on a Quest 3 (cheap, a few days) and (b) the live end-to-end demo with photodiode motion-to-photon latency and the user study, which need a small 6-8 camera synced rig, an edge GPU and WiFi 6 with network emulation (tc/netem). Reviewers at IEEE VR/ISMAR will expect (b).

review.first_two_week_test: Run offline emulation on DyNeRF (2 scenes) plus ActorsHQ (2 actors, dense cameras) with no network or headset. Days 1-3: record about 10 minutes of seated-conversation 6DoF head traces on a Quest 3, or use any logged HMD traces, and compute constant-velocity or Kalman prediction residuals at horizons of 33, 66, 100 and 150 ms. Days 3-8: for each held-out camera p, build virtual predicted poses p̂ = p − Δ from the residuals. Render RGB-D at p̂ with the same IBR colour (base pipeline if code is available, otherwise a simple visibility-weighted blend) under three depth sources: (i) per-frame stereo/MVS depth, (ii) per-frame depth plus a temporal filter, (iii) image-based TSDF fused over views and time. Then forward-warp a single layer to p. Days 8-12: add a naive second layer from multi-hit TSDF raymarching with nearest-visible-camera colour. Measure LPIPS versus GT at p, hole rate, and flow-warping flicker on a fixed p while p̂ jitters with the trace. Also measure the same depth sources rendered directly at p, which is the 'invisible' condition. Days 12-14: plot flicker and LPIPS against prediction horizon, and compare against a post-hoc EMA deflicker on the raw-depth output. Success means the consistency gap is large under reprojection (≥30% flicker reduction at 66-100 ms), small without reprojection, and grows with horizon, and EMA does not close it without introducing ghosting. Also establish at what horizon layer 2 cuts the hole rate meaningfully.
review.kill_criteria: Drop or pivot if any of these hold. (1) At realistic horizons (66-100 ms) consistent depth reduces displayed flicker by less than about 15% relative, or the gap does not grow with horizon; the central claim is then false. (2) A trivial post-hoc temporal EMA or deflicker on raw-depth reprojection matches consistent depth within noise, without visible ghosting. (3) Translational pose error at 100 ms under conversational head motion is so small (for example below 1 cm, sub-pixel disocclusions) that rotational timewarp plus a wider FoV matches the layered bundle. In that case drop the layer and bundle story and keep only the consistency-under-reprojection finding as a short paper or benchmark section. (4) Client-side rendering of streamed per-frame Gaussians or meshes (2604.02851- or MeshReduce-style) reaches equal quality at equal or lower bitrate within the Quest 3 budget; the bundle then has no Pareto advantage. (5) Before month 3, a 2026 paper appears that measures reprojection shimmer of live-captured people with consistent depth.

reviewer_objections.objection: This is QuadStream/PVS/MIV plus MeshReduce applied to telepresence. Split rendering with layered disocclusion-robust representations and view cells is old, so this is engineering.
reviewer_objections.rebuttal: We concede the architecture and cite it as such. The contribution is what those works cannot observe: with estimated, noisy depth of live people, the dominant artefact is display-rate shimmer, not holes, and it scales with prediction horizon times depth temporal noise. We quantify this, show that consistency-fused depth plus reprojection-aware training fixes it, and show that QuadStream/MIV-style layering with raw depth does not. Hidden layers are estimated and IBR-shaded from real cameras rather than rasterised from a G-buffer.

reviewer_objections.objection: Head translation over 50-100 ms is only a few centimetres. Rotational ATW/ASW already solves latency, and depth layers are unnecessary.
reviewer_objections.rebuttal: We measure this directly with recorded Quest 3 conversational traces and report hole rate and flicker against horizon, including the break-even point for layer 2. Over WiFi/5G plus a 33 ms render, horizons of 80-150 ms are common. Even where layers turn out unnecessary, depth-based (not rotational) warping is needed for parallax on near-field faces at 0.5-1.5 m, and depth consistency matters there regardless of layer count. The paper's main claim does not depend on layers.

reviewer_objections.objection: Why not stream a 3D representation (per-frame Gaussians, mesh) and render fully on the client, as in 2604.02851, MeshReduce or SqueezeMe?
reviewer_objections.rebuttal: We include these as baselines on a bitrate / client-ms / quality Pareto. Dense per-view Gaussians from an 8-camera rig amount to millions of splats per frame, which strains Quest 3 bandwidth and GPU. Meshes lose view-dependent IBR appearance and hair. The bundle's per-vsync client cost is fixed (under 3 ms) whatever the scene complexity. If a baseline dominates, we report it; the consistency-under-reprojection result remains useful to those pipelines too.

reviewer_objections.objection: Ground truth at display rate and at arbitrary head poses does not exist, so the evaluation is unconvincing.
reviewer_objections.rebuttal: Dense rigs (ActorsHQ 160 cams, Panoptic) give ground truth at many true poses near each predicted pose. Pose errors are sampled from real head-trace residuals, so reprojected output is compared against real images. Display-rate flicker uses established GT-free measures (flow-warping error, FovVideoVDP), and a user study with 2AFC flicker preference and SSQ on the live system closes the loop. We will release the protocol and traces as a benchmark.

reviewer_objections.objection: The base paper's own ablation shows the TSDF barely matters (31.16 vs 31.17 dB), so why expect depth consistency to matter here?
reviewer_objections.rebuttal: That is the hypothesis being tested. Direct rendering at the true pose hides depth error because the IBR blend is tolerant to it, whereas reprojection turns depth error into pixel motion in proportion to pose error. We predict and test an interaction: a near-zero effect without reprojection and a large effect with it. Confirming this interaction also explains why standard NVS benchmarks undervalue geometry consistency for telepresence.

effort.months: 7-9 (2 weeks go/no-go emulation; about 3 months offline method and reprojection-aware training on public data; 2-3 months Quest 3 client, live rig integration and latency measurement; about 1.5 months user study and writing)
effort.people: 2 (one PhD student on the vision/learning side: depth consistency, layered IBR, training; one on systems/graphics: Quest 3 Vulkan/OpenXR warper, codec, network emulation, photodiode rig). One person is feasible only if the live system is cut to a minimal demo.
effort.compute: 1-2 RTX 4090 / A6000-class GPUs for training and the edge server; about 2-4 GPU-weeks total. Plus a Quest 3 (optionally Vision Pro), a WiFi 6 router with netem, a photodiode or oscilloscope, and a 6-8 camera synced stereo or RGB-D rig (about $5-15k) for the live demo.

review.venue: Primary: IEEE ISMAR 2027 (TVCG journal track), since the IEEE VR 2027 deadline has effectively passed and the next realistic target is IEEE VR 2028. The emphasis should be the displayed-stream consistency finding, the Quest 3 system and the user study. Alternative: SIGGRAPH Asia 2027 (TOG) if reprojection-aware training yields large, clean gains and the analysis is strong. Avoid CVPR unless the systems part is reduced to a benchmark and protocol contribution.
review.synergies: (1) Moving and binocular viewer consistency (left/right stereo consistency plus a view x time consistency benchmark): the reprojected-display metric and the dense-rig reprojected-GT protocol are the same infrastructure, so this could become a single benchmark paper plus this method paper. (2) Split sender/receiver compute placement (what to transmit: RGB-D vs Gaussians vs latents): this work supplies the latency and consistency axis of that trade-off, and the pose-uncertainty-sized bundle is one point in the design space. (3) Glass-to-glass latency measurement for online 3D video: the photodiode motion-to-photon harness is reusable. (4) Robust RGB-D rigs (flying pixels, ToF interference): noisy silhouette depth is exactly what drives reprojection shimmer, so a depth-cleaning front end plugs straight in. (5) Streaming one-step diffusion or transformer fixers (e.g. the real-time 3D streaming inpainting of arXiv 2603.05507): a lightweight client- or edge-side disocclusion filler for residual holes. (6) Foveated telepresence compression: guard-band and layer budgets can be foveated using headset eye tracking. A paper series could run: benchmark/metric (display-rate consistency) -> this method -> compute-split optimisation.

name: Room-as-light-probe: live relighting of remote participant into receiver lighting using the sender rig TSDF room radiance

cited_work_check.title: LiveLight: Real-time Streaming Video Relighting with Interactive Control (TOG 2026)
cited_work_check.note: Submitted 3 Aug 2026 and accepted to TOG 2026. It is real-time streaming diffusion relighting driven by user-controlled Multi-Plane Light Irradiance maps; target lighting is user-specified, not observed. The abstract does not say 'monocular', but the method is single-stream video with no multi-view consistency, so the ideator's description is fair.

cited_work_check.title: Relightable Holoported Characters: Capturing and Relighting Dynamic Human Performance from Sparse Views
cited_work_check.note: By Singh, Chen, Golyanik, Garbin, Beeler, Dabral, Habermann and Theobalt; Nov 2025, revised Mar 2026. Feed-forward RelightNet from sparse views. It needs a new multi-view lightstage capture and dataset, and makes no real-time claim. Matches the ideator's description.

cited_work_check.title: EgoRelight: Egocentric Human Capture and Illumination Recovery for Relightable and Photoreal Avatar Rendering (TOG 2026)
cited_work_check.note: Exists (27 May 2026; also TOG, doi 10.1145/3811346). The ideator undersells it. It already scans the sender's own room (about 10 s of HMD front-camera capture, 20 images, a 3D reconstruction unprojected to a panorama, diffusion inpainting, then an inverse-rendering LDR-to-HDR step that uses the user's own relightable avatar as calibration target). It then shows telepresence with 'User 1 inserted into User 2's real environment' and coherently relit. That is the sender-room-as-light-probe plus relight-into-receiver concept, although it is avatar-based, person-specific, lightstage-trained, and uses a far-field env map rather than near-field geometry.

cited_work_check.title: LightBridge: Feed-Forward Generative Relighting for 3D Gaussian Splatting
cited_work_check.note: Submitted 2 Sep 2026 (Cao, ..., Ligang Liu). Feed-forward relighting of static 3DGS assets with a multi-illumination dataset, as the ideator claims.

cited_work_check.title: Real-time 3D-aware Portrait Video Relighting (CVPR 2024 Highlight)
cited_work_check.note: Monocular talking-face relighting with tri-planes at about 33 fps, plus a temporal consistency network. Accurate.

cited_work_check.title: Comprehensive Relighting: Generalizable and Consistent Monocular Human Relighting and Harmonization (CVPR 2025)
cited_work_check.note: Monocular diffusion-based human relighting and harmonization with an unsupervised temporal lighting model; not multi-view. Accurate.

threats.title: EgoRelight: Egocentric Human Capture and Illumination Recovery for Relightable and Photoreal Avatar Rendering
threats.what_overlaps: It reconstructs the sender's own room from device cameras (a 3D scene built from a 360-degree scan and unprojected to a panorama), lifts it to HDR by inverse rendering against the person's appearance, and uses this recovered lighting to relight the remote participant into the receiver's real environment in a mixed-reality telepresence demo. This is the problem statement, the 'observe the sender's surroundings so source lighting is measured, not guessed' insight, and the relight-into-receiver application.
threats.what_remains_different: It is avatar-based and person-specific, and needs multi-view lightstage training per identity. The room is a one-off 10 s scan collapsed to a far-field env map, not a continuously updated near-field, spatially varying radiance field. There is no image-based rendering of live multi-view RGB-D, no identity-agnostic feed-forward de-lighting, no multi-view or stereo consistency of relit IBR output, no TSDF-anchored temporal albedo memory, and no end-to-end latency claim (only the avatar runs at 46 FPS).

threats.title: Multi-view Inverse Rendering for Large-scale Real-world Indoor Scenes (TexIR, texture-based lighting)
threats.what_overlaps: It establishes that a reconstructed room mesh with HDR textures is the near-field incident illumination ('scene geometry itself as the lighting source'), which is exactly the 'room radiance IS the light probe' idea. Related static-scene work such as NeILF++ (https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.17147) does the same with inter-reflectable light fields.
threats.what_remains_different: Offline and static-scene only; it recovers the scene's own materials and does not de-light a dynamic human inside the room in real time. Applying the scene-as-emitter model to a live person in a telepresence rig is new.

threats.title: URAvatar: Universal Relightable Gaussian Codec Avatars
threats.what_overlaps: Real-time relightable head avatars personalised from a phone scan by inverse-rendering fine-tuning. This implicitly factors out the capture environment's lighting and supports relighting under arbitrary environments, which is the Codec-Avatar route to 'relight the remote person into the receiver's lighting'. The full-body version (https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.14726, SIGGRAPH 2025) extends this.
threats.what_remains_different: Avatar and prior-model based (lightstage training over hundreds of identities), with no live multi-view IBR and no use of the sender room as an explicit near-field light probe.

threats.title: BEAM: Bridging Physically-based Rendering and Gaussian Modeling for Relightable Volumetric Video
threats.what_overlaps: Recovers geometry and materials from multi-view RGB footage to produce relightable volumetric video, with real-time deferred-shading playback, and explicitly names telepresence as an application.
threats.what_remains_different: Per-sequence optimisation (offline reconstruction); it does not use the observed room as the source light and is not an online, feed-forward pipeline.

threats.title: Real-time Shadow-aware Portrait Relighting in Virtual Backgrounds for Realistic Telepresence
threats.what_overlaps: Real-time relighting of a telepresence participant to match a new (virtual) background, i.e. a lighting-consistent composite for telepresence.
threats.what_remains_different: Single-view 2D portrait into virtual backgrounds; no multi-view or 3D consistency and no observed room light probe.

threats.title: Hybrelighter: Combining Deep Anisotropic Diffusion and Scene Reconstruction for On-device Real-time Relighting in Mixed Reality
threats.what_overlaps: Uses on-device scene reconstruction to drive real-time (up to 100 fps) relighting in MR on the headset.
threats.what_remains_different: Relights the local physical room under virtual lights, not a remote human, and uses no source-light de-lighting.

threats.title: Relit-LiVE: Relight Video by Jointly Learning Environment Video
threats.what_overlaps: Jointly predicts per-frame environment maps aligned with each viewpoint and relit video, so source and target lighting are explicit.
threats.what_remains_different: Diffusion, offline, monocular or moving camera; it infers the environment rather than observing it with a calibrated rig.

threats.title: LiveLight: Real-time Streaming Video Relighting with Interactive Control
threats.what_overlaps: Real-time streaming, temporally coherent relighting with depth-aware multi-plane irradiance conditioning.
threats.what_remains_different: Single stream, user-specified lights, no observed source illumination, no cross-view or stereo consistency.

threats.title: Relightable Holoported Characters
threats.what_overlaps: Feed-forward relighting of dynamic humans from sparse multi-view video.
threats.what_remains_different: Lightstage-captured training data, tracked mesh proxy, not live, and no room light probe.

threats.title: Deep Relightable Textures / The Relightables
threats.what_overlaps: Relightable volumetric performance capture of humans for free-viewpoint playback.
threats.what_remains_different: Custom lightstage with active illumination; no passive room-as-probe de-lighting.

novelty.remaining_novel_angle: The most defensible claim is identity-agnostic, lightstage-free, online relighting of live image-based-rendered multi-view RGB-D telepresence video. Source illumination is taken from a continuously updated, near-field, spatially varying radiance field built from the sender rig's TSDF room reconstruction, instead of a per-person relightable avatar (EgoRelight, URAvatar) or a hallucinated environment map (LiveLight, Relit-LiVE, Comprehensive Relighting). Relit output is kept consistent across views, eyes and time by a TSDF-anchored albedo memory gated by the base paper's static/dynamic masks. The lamp-switching paired multi-illumination capture on the same rig is a secondary contribution that nobody else claims. What is NOT novel: (a) 'reconstructed room radiance is the incident near-field light' (TexIR CVPR 2023, NeILF++); (b) 'observe the sender's surroundings to recover source lighting, then relight the remote user into the receiver's environment for MR telepresence' (EgoRelight, TOG 2026, which does exactly this with an HMD room scan). The paper must position against EgoRelight explicitly. The key differentiators are no per-user lightstage model, near-field and time-varying source light, live IBR, and multi-view or stereo consistency. Technical caveat that weakens the 'well-posed de-lighting' pitch: a telepresence rig's cameras face the person, so they mostly observe the room behind and around the subject, while the frontal hemisphere behind the cameras (usually containing the key light, screen and ceiling fixtures) goes unobserved. The light probe is therefore largely incomplete exactly where the dominant illumination comes from, and needs learned completion or dedicated outward-facing cameras. Reviewers will raise this, so the claim should be softened to 'partially observed, better-constrained' source lighting.
novelty.best_variant: The cluster has a single idea (Room-as-Light-Probe), so the question is which of its components is most defensible. The strongest core is the combination of three things: (1) near-field, time-varying source lighting from the rig's own TSDF room radiance, used in a feed-forward, identity-agnostic de-lighting network; (2) a TSDF-anchored temporal albedo memory that turns relighting flicker into the base paper's temporal-filtering problem; (3) cross-view and stereo-consistent relit IBR output. This combination survives against EgoRelight, which is avatar-based, lightstage-trained, uses a far-field one-off scan and claims no end-to-end latency. The 'first live AR telepresence relit into receiver lighting' contribution should be dropped or heavily qualified, because EgoRelight already demonstrates relighting remote users into the receiver's physical environment for MR telepresence. The lamp-switching paired-data capture should be kept as a secondary dataset or benchmark contribution. To make the probe claim credible, the paper should also measure how much of the incident sphere a typical rig actually observes, and add a completion module or a cheap outward-facing camera.

sharpened.title: Rig-as-Light-Stage: De-lighting Live Multi-View Telepresence Video with Observed Near-Field Illumination and a Known Display Emitter
sharpened.one_liner: A calibrated telepresence booth measures a large share of its own lighting. It sees the room through its TSDF and knows exactly what its display is emitting. Conditioning a feed-forward, identity-agnostic intrinsic network on that observed source light gives albedo that is more accurate and more consistent across views, eyes and time than lighting estimated from images, and that albedo can then be relit into the receiver's lighting within about 25 ms.
sharpened.core_claim: The comparison holds everything fixed except how the source lighting is obtained. On a matched network and data budget, conditioning de-lighting on rig-observed source illumination (HDR TSDF room radiance, the per-frame known display emission and a learned completion of the unobserved directions) should beat image-estimated lighting (a single-image or panorama estimator, or an EgoRelight-style far-field env map collapsed from the same room scan). It should (a) cut scale-invariant albedo error by at least 20% and relit LPIPS by at least 15% against paired ground truth, (b) cut cross-view and left/right albedo inconsistency and temporal flicker by at least 30%, and (c) add no more than 25 ms per frame on a single RTX 4090-class GPU. If observed lighting does not beat estimated lighting by at least 10% on (a), the central thesis is false.
sharpened.key_insight: De-lighting from images is ill-posed because the incident light is a latent variable. A fixed, calibrated booth is an unusual case where much of that variable can be measured. Behind and around the subject, the rig's TSDF holds the room's near-field, spatially varying radiance. In front of the subject, where the rig cannot see and where the key light normally is, the booth's own display is a large area emitter whose radiance is known exactly on every frame because the system renders it. The display also varies over time, so it acts as a free, passive active-illumination signal, like 'A Light Stage on Every Desk'. What remains unobserved (ceiling fixtures, lamps behind the display) is small, and its size can be measured. The problem changes from guessing all of the lighting to completing a known, measured residual. Once albedo is recovered this way, it varies slowly and is anchored to the TSDF surface. The base paper's static/dynamic masks and previous-frame depth feedback therefore become an albedo memory, and relighting flicker reduces to the temporal-filtering problem the pipeline already solves.
sharpened.method: (0) Session setup, about 30 s, once per session. Capture an exposure-bracketed sweep of the empty room with the rig cameras, plus an optional cheap outward-facing fisheye mounted on the display bezel. Fuse the result into an HDR-radiance TSDF. Detect saturated emitters and calibrate their intensity from the brackets. Radiometrically calibrate the display once (per-pixel radiance as a function of RGB value, using a phone lux meter or a colour chart). (1) Source-light field. Build a coarse 3D probe grid over the person volume, for example 6x6x6 probes, each holding 32 spherical-Gaussian lobes or L2 spherical harmonics plus a per-lobe visibility and observedness mask. The room term is rendered from the TSDF radiance mesh and refreshed only where the static mask changes, so its cost is amortised. The display term is added every frame from a 16x9 downsampled frame buffer treated as area lights, which is linear and cheap. A small completion network (a 3D CNN on the lobe grid) in-paints the unobserved lobes. It is trained on synthetic rooms and outputs uncertainty. (2) Intrinsic network. It shares its encoder with the base paper's 4-level blend U-Net. For each warped input view it takes the warped RGB, the TSDF normals and depth, the irradiance E_src(x) sampled from the grid, the dominant-lobe directions and the observedness. It predicts albedo A, a residual R (specular, occlusion and shadow error) and a confidence c, with the image-formation constraint I ≈ A·E_src + R. (3) TSDF- and reprojection-anchored albedo memory. Background albedo is fused into TSDF voxels. Person albedo comes from the previous frame, reprojected with the base paper's previous-frame depth feedback and fused by an EMA gated by the difference mask M and the confidence c. A lighting-invariant variant of M, computed on A instead of RGB, fixes the base paper's known failure of confusing 'moved' with 're-lit'. (4) Target light. Use the receiver's own booth TSDF when both ends are symmetric booths, or a real-time HMD-passthrough lighting estimator in AR, expressed in the same probe grid. (5) Re-render. I' = A·E_tgt + h(R, target lobes, view direction), where h is a small residual network. The relit views are blended with the existing geometry-guided weights, which keeps them consistent across views and eyes by construction. An optional contact shadow is cast onto the receiver's floor. Training data: (i) path-traced synthetic booths. These are Blender rooms plus textured human scans or rigged assets with albedo, rendered with an 8-12 camera frontal arc, an emissive display playing video content, randomised lamps and GT albedo, irradiance and relit targets. (ii) Public multi-view multi-illumination humans (HumanOLAT, UltraStage) composited under room-derived lighting for real-skin supervision. (iii) A small real paired capture on a 6-8 camera rig. DMX or smart LED panels are strobed on alternate frames and synchronised to the camera trigger (Relightables-style), and slow lamp and display-content changes give paired illuminations. Losses: relit L1+LPIPS; albedo L1 (synthetic); the reconstruction constraint I = A·E_src + R on unpaired real data; cross-view albedo consistency via depth reprojection; a temporal albedo warp loss; a sparsity prior on R. Runtime budget: about 5 ms for the probe grid (display term plus amortised room term), 10-15 ms for the intrinsic head on the shared encoder, and about 5 ms for relighting and blending. That is 20-25 ms on top of the base pipeline's 40-100 ms. Scope is limited to upper-body participants and to diffuse lighting plus a learned residual; accurate eye and glasses specularity is out of scope.
sharpened.why_not_engineering: The paper tests a measurable hypothesis about an inverse problem: whether partially observed near-field illumination, plus one exactly known emitter, makes feed-forward de-lighting of humans better constrained than learned lighting estimation, and by how much in terms of observed solid-angle and irradiance coverage. It supplies the analysis tools: an irradiance-coverage study across rig layouts and rooms showing how much of the subject's incident light a booth actually observes, and an ablation ladder (estimated, far-field-from-scan, near-field, plus display, plus completion) that isolates each source of constraint. The known display emitter as passive active illumination for live de-lighting is a new observation for telepresence booths. The lighting-invariant static/dynamic gating (masks on albedo, not RGB) is a principled fix for a documented failure mode of the base method. It is not a bolt-on filter. There is also a benchmark contribution: paired multi-illumination multi-view dynamic video of people in real rooms with room scans, for which no public equivalent exists.
sharpened.differentiation: EgoRelight (arXiv 2605.28401, TOG 2026) already shows the concept of observing the sender's surroundings, recovering HDR lighting and relighting the remote user into the receiver's room. It does this with a person-specific, lightstage-trained avatar and a one-off far-field env map, driven from an HMD. This work is identity-agnostic image-based rendering of live multi-view RGB-D. Its source light is near-field, spatially varying and time-varying, and it includes the known display emitter, which covers exactly the frontal hemisphere an HMD room scan also misses. The paper will not claim 'first relit telepresence'. It will include an 'EgoRelight-style far-field' ablation built from the same room scan to show that near-field matters. URAvatar and the Relightable Full-Body Gaussian Codec Avatars are avatar- and prior-based, need lightstage pretraining and per-user enrolment, and use no live IBR. Relightable Holoported Characters (arXiv 2512.00255) and GRGS (arXiv 2505.21502) are feed-forward multi-view human relighting methods, but they are trained on lightstage data, are not live and estimate or assume source lighting rather than observing it. TexIR (arXiv 2211.10206) and NeILF++ use the scene as a near-field emitter, but offline, on static scenes and for the scene's own materials. This work applies the scene-as-emitter model to a dynamic person, live. LiveLight (arXiv 2608.01771), Comprehensive Relighting (arXiv 2504.03011), Lux Post Facto and IC-Light-style relighters are monocular, work from hallucinated or user-specified lighting and are not cross-view or stereo consistent; they are baselines. A Light Stage on Every Desk (arXiv 2105.08051) uses a monitor as a light stage for single-view faces with per-user training. This work generalises the idea to a multi-view booth, combines it with room radiance, and runs it identity-agnostically in real time. The ISMAR 2022 shadow-aware telepresence relighting paper is single-view and targets virtual backgrounds.

experiments.capture_notes: No public dataset has dynamic multi-view people in ordinary rooms with paired illuminations and a room scan, so custom capture is unavoidable for the real evaluation. The minimum viable rig is 6-8 global-shutter or RGB-D cameras on a frontal arc (hardware-synchronised), one monitor as the display emitter, 2-4 DMX or controllable LED panels triggered in sync with the cameras to strobe alternate lighting at 60 fps (flow-align adjacent frames for pairs), and one outward-facing fisheye. Add HDR bracket scans of each room and a colour chart. Budget is about $4-8k, a small lab room, IRB consent for 6-10 subjects, and about 2 capture weeks. The synthetic benchmark and the OLAT composites carry most of the quantitative claims; the real paired set validates transfer. Plan for strobing discomfort (use slow alternation or held poses as a fallback).

review.first_two_week_test: Build a probe-coverage and oracle-shading study in Blender, with no network training. Use 3 rooms from free Blender or Poly Haven scenes, 3 lighting setups each (ceiling fixture, desk lamp behind the display, window), 5 textured human scans, an 8-camera frontal arc and an emissive 27-inch display playing video. Render GT albedo, normals, irradiance and images. For each subject surface point, compute the incident irradiance split into three parts: directions observed by the rig cameras in the TSDF, the display, and unobserved directions. Report the observed fraction. Then solve albedo in closed form (A = (I - 0)/E) with GT normals and five irradiance sources: (a) observed room only, (b) observed room plus display, (c) (b) plus naive completion (mean fill or nearest observed lobe), (d) an off-the-shelf single-image or panorama lighting estimate from one rig camera, and (e) GT. Compare scale-invariant albedo error and cross-view albedo consistency. Proceed if (b) or (c) captures at least 60% of irradiance in typical setups and beats (d) by at least 20% in albedo error. If a real rig is at hand, take one bonus sanity check: switch a monitor between white and black while a person sits still, and confirm that the predicted display-only irradiance difference explains most of the observed pixel change on the face (R² above about 0.7).
review.kill_criteria: Drop or pivot if any of the following holds. (1) In realistic booth layouts, observed room plus display accounts for less than about 50% of subject irradiance, and completing the rest does not beat a single-image lighting estimator by at least 10% in albedo error; the 'observed source light' thesis then fails, so pivot to plain harmonisation or drop. (2) With a matched network, observed-light conditioning improves relit LPIPS and albedo error by less than 10% over estimated-light conditioning on the synthetic and OLAT benchmarks. (3) The pipeline cannot keep overhead under about 30 ms, or cross-view and temporal consistency is not at least 30% better than per-view diffusion relighters. (4) After 4 months, per-view diffusion relighting (IC-Light or LiveLight-style) is preferred in the AR 2AFC more than 60% of the time despite its inconsistency; the practical value then lies in a generative refiner, not in this route. (5) A new paper appears that does identity-agnostic live multi-view relighting with observed room lighting.

reviewer_objections.objection: EgoRelight (TOG 2026) already recovers the sender's environment lighting from a room scan and relights remote users into the receiver's room for telepresence, so the concept is not new.
reviewer_objections.rebuttal: Agreed on the concept, and the paper says so. The contribution is different: identity-agnostic, no per-user lightstage, live IBR of arbitrary people, near-field, spatially varying and time-varying source light rather than a one-off far-field env map, and the known display emitter covering the frontal hemisphere. A controlled 'far-field from the same scan' ablation, which is EgoRelight's lighting model, quantifies the gain from near-field and display terms.

reviewer_objections.objection: The rig's cameras face the subject, so the dominant frontal and overhead light is unobserved. The 'observed light probe' is mostly missing where it matters, and the problem is still ill-posed.
reviewer_objections.rebuttal: This is measured directly with the coverage study across layouts and rooms, and the claim is limited to 'better constrained', not 'well-posed'. The frontal hemisphere is partly covered by the display, whose radiance is known exactly, and optionally by a cheap outward fisheye. The rest is completed by a network with explicit uncertainty. The ablation ladder shows how much each term helps and where it fails.

reviewer_objections.objection: LDR cameras cannot measure emitter radiance; saturated lamps make the HDR room radiance, and hence the source irradiance, wrong by large factors.
reviewer_objections.rebuttal: The rig is fixed and the room is static, so a one-time exposure-bracketed scan at session start gives HDR radiance for lamps. The display is calibrated once. The paper reports sensitivity to single-exposure LDR plus inverse tone mapping versus bracketing, and treats albedo scale ambiguity with scale-invariant metrics plus a global white-balance and exposure term.

reviewer_objections.objection: This is an intrinsic-decomposition-plus-shading engineering stack. Modern diffusion relighters (LiveLight, IC-Light, DiffusionRenderer) produce far better-looking relighting.
reviewer_objections.rebuttal: Diffusion relighters hallucinate source lighting and are not consistent across views or eyes, which is fatal in stereo AR. This is measured with consistency metrics and in the user study. The scientific question is the value of observed illumination, and the observed-light conditioning is complementary: it can feed a one-step generative refiner later. Diffusion baselines are included at their best settings.

reviewer_objections.objection: The evaluation rests on synthetic data and a small custom capture; there is no established benchmark, and the telepresence benefit of relighting is unproven.
reviewer_objections.rebuttal: Three tiers of evidence: a synthetic benchmark with full GT, real public multi-view OLAT humans (HumanOLAT, UltraStage) with composited lighting, and a released real paired-illumination multi-view booth dataset. On top of that, an AR co-presence user study. Prior telepresence work (ISMAR 2022 shadow-aware relighting, EgoRelight) establishes that lighting mismatch matters.

effort.months: 10-12 (2 for synthetic plus coverage study, 2 for capture rig and data, 4-5 for the model, memory and real-time integration, 2 for the user study and writing)
effort.people: 2 (one PhD student on inverse rendering and learning, one on the rig, capture and AR system); a single student would need about 15 months or a reduced scope that drops the AR study
effort.compute: 2-4 GPUs of 24-80 GB for about 2-3 GPU-weeks of training in total; path-traced synthetic data generation is the main cost (about 50-100k multi-view frames on a small render farm or cloud); an RTX 4090 for real-time demos; $4-8k capture hardware (6-8 synced cameras, LED panels with DMX or trigger, a fisheye, a monitor, colour charts)

review.venue: IEEE VR 2027 / ISMAR 2027 (journal track, TVCG) as the most realistic target, given the system, user-study and consistency framing. SIGGRAPH Asia 2027 (TOG) is a stretch if the coverage analysis plus the real paired benchmark are strong. CVPR 2027 is possible only if framed as a de-lighting and benchmark paper with strong quantitative gains over estimated-lighting baselines.
review.synergies: (1) Motion- and lighting-aware static/dynamic separation (landscape gap: the base paper's colour-difference mask confuses 'moved' with 're-lit'). Albedo-space masks from this work solve that directly, so the two could merge into one paper or form a series. (2) Persistent TSDF or Gaussian state in the wire format, where static content is sent once and dynamic residuals are streamed. Transmitting albedo and normals once plus per-frame dynamic residuals makes relighting at the receiver natural and cuts bitrate, a strong joint 'relightable streaming state' story. (3) A streaming one-step generative fixer inside the IBR loop (landscape gap). The observed-light G-buffers (A, E_src, E_tgt, normals) are ideal conditioning for a distilled relight or refine model, combining physical consistency with generative quality. (4) Handling view-dependent and specular appearance, a known weakness of the base paper. The residual branch R is a first step toward it. (5) Geometry foundation models and depth priors (MapAnything, Video Depth Anything, Stereo Any Video). Better normals directly reduce shading error. (6) AR compositing, occlusion and contact shadows at the receiver, and co-presence user-study infrastructure shared with other telepresence directions.

cited_work_check.title: A Multi-View 3D Telepresence System for XR Robot Teleoperation (Dincer et al., 2026)
cited_work_check.note: Mostly accurate: 3 static RGB-D cameras fused into about 75k-point clouds at 10 Hz on Quest 3, a floating wrist-RGB window and a 31-person within-subject study. However, the claim of 'no robot-aware fusion' is wrong. The HTML full text says the robot, gripper and camera mount are segmented out of the clouds with YOLOv11, because the robot is already rendered as meshes from the Panda URDF in Unity. The paper also describes 'foveated RGB detail'. So robot-aware geometry handling and foveation are partly done already; only the method differs (learned segmentation rather than kinematic projection into a TSDF).

cited_work_check.note: GS-SLAM integrated into a map-based teleoperation stack, demonstrated on aerial vehicles. It targets mostly static mapping, as the ideator says.

cited_work_check.title: AnyCamVLA: Zero-Shot Camera Adaptation for VLA models (2026)
cited_work_check.note: Feed-forward NVS used to re-render test-time observations into the training viewpoints for VLA policies. Characterised correctly as serving a policy, not a human display.

threats.title: Physically Embodied Gaussian Splatting: A Realtime Correctable World Model for Robotics (Embodied Gaussians)
threats.what_overlaps: The render-and-compare core insight. It renders the predicted state from 3 calibrated cameras, compares it with the observed images and uses the residual ('visual forces') to correct a particle and Gaussian world model at 30 Hz, with robot state and physical constraints built in. Robot-state-aware prediction plus a render-vs-observe residual already appears here in a real-time robotics setting.
threats.what_remains_different: Its goal is state estimation and simulation, not photoreal free-viewpoint video for a human operator. It needs per-object particle and Gaussian initialisation, cannot handle novel or unmodelled content, has no feed-forward IBR, no moving (wrist) cameras, and no temporal-consistency metrics or teleoperation user study.

threats.title: ReFusion: 3D Reconstruction in Dynamic Environments for RGB-D Cameras Exploiting Residuals
threats.what_overlaps: Detects dynamic content in TSDF fusion with a moving RGB-D camera from residuals between the rendered model and the observed depth and colour after registration, plus free-space modelling. This is the 'ego-motion-invariant render-and-compare mask' idea in classical form. StaticFusion and Co-Fusion are in the same line.
threats.what_remains_different: It is a single-camera SLAM map that removes dynamic content rather than rendering it. There is no multi-camera IBR, no learned blending, and no use of known kinematic poses or robot meshes.

threats.title: Human-in-the-loop Gaussian Splatting for Robotic Teleoperation (HIL-GS)
threats.what_overlaps: Teleoperation display built from a robot-mounted, moving RGB-D camera whose motion comes from proprioception ('motion-aware reconstruction combining RGB-D and proprioceptive sensors'). The GS is updated inside the teleoperation loop (Scholar snippet: 10k Gaussian updates at 2 Hz) and shown in VR with a user evaluation.
threats.what_remains_different: Online-optimised GS mapping at about 2 Hz, aimed at mostly static scenes. It has no fixed-rig and moving-camera fusion, no per-frame feed-forward rendering of a changing workspace, no temporal-consistency mechanism and no robot-mesh geometry prior at contact. (Abstract read via Google Scholar only; full text not opened.)

threats.title: Toward Real-time High-fidelity Immersive Robotic Telepresence via Online 3D Gaussian Splatting
threats.what_overlaps: Online 3DGS VR robotic telepresence, co-designed for fidelity, latency and convergence speed. It occupies the 'photoreal, live-ish 3D robot telepresence' framing the idea claims is missing.
threats.what_remains_different: Per-scene online optimisation that grows with the scene, framed around telepresence and exploration. There is no evidence of dynamic manipulated objects, feed-forward per-frame IBR, kinematic robot-geometry fusion or temporal-consistency evaluation (abstract only).

threats.title: A Multi-View 3D Telepresence System for XR Robot Teleoperation
threats.what_overlaps: The exact application setting: fixed multi-view RGB-D plus a wrist camera for manipulation teleoperation, the robot removed from sensor geometry and re-rendered from the URDF, foveated RGB detail, and a 31-person manipulation user study against RGB, stereo and point-cloud baselines.
threats.what_remains_different: Point clouds only (the authors call them 'visually fuzzy at edges'). The wrist camera is used as a 2D panel rather than fused geometrically, there is no photoreal IBR and no temporal filtering or consistency, and robot removal uses YOLO segmentation rather than kinematic projection into the fusion.

threats.title: Reality Promises: Virtual-Physical Decoupling Illusions in Mixed Reality via Invisible Mobile Robots
threats.what_overlaps: 'Robot-aware 3D Gaussian splat rasterization' driven by live joint states streamed to the HMD. Using kinematics inside a Gaussian renderer is already done, though here it is used to hide the robot.
threats.what_remains_different: Diminished-reality illusion, not geometry fusion for accurate depth at gripper-object contact, and not teleoperation.

threats.title: Isaac ROS cuMotion robot segmenter + nvblox (engineering prior art)
threats.what_overlaps: Segments and filters the robot out of depth streams using its kinematic model before GPU TSDF fusion (nvblox). The idea's 'mask robot pixels out of sensor depth' step is therefore standard practice.
threats.what_remains_different: Used for collision mapping. It does not insert the robot mesh as high-confidence geometry into an image-space TSDF for IBR, and there is no rendering.

threats.title: GHOST in the Robots: Real-Time Exocentric Dual-Robot VR Teleoperation from Onboard Cameras
threats.what_overlaps: Builds a live exocentric 3D workspace from moving, robot-onboard RGB-D cameras, aligned in real time with learning-based completion, for VR manipulation teleoperation.
threats.what_remains_different: Point-cloud representation with no photoreal IBR, no fixed rig, and no temporal-consistency or robot-mesh depth fusion.

threats.title: Immersive remote telerobotics: foveated unicasting and remote visualization for intuitive interaction
threats.what_overlaps: Foveated rendering and streaming for immersive teleoperation around the manipulation region. Undercuts 'task-aware foveation' as a standalone contribution.
threats.what_remains_different: No geometry-guided multi-view IBR, and no end-effector-centric view selection for blending.

threats.title: Low-Latency Telepresence via Gaussian Splatting With Safety-Aware Control for Mobile Manipulators
threats.what_overlaps: Arm-mounted camera whose viewpoint comes from forward kinematics, with on-demand GS reconstruction for low-latency local rendering in telepresence.
threats.what_remains_different: On-demand static reconstruction of museum-like scenes. There is no dynamic manipulation workspace and no fusion with a fixed rig.

novelty.remaining_novel_angle:
Each claimed technical ingredient has prior art taken on its own. Render-and-compare residual masks for moving-camera TSDF fusion go back to ReFusion and StaticFusion, and render-vs-observed correction with robot state at 30 Hz is Embodied Gaussians. Kinematic robot self-filtering from depth is standard (cuMotion/nvblox), and Dincer et al. 2026 already remove the robot from the fused geometry and re-render it from the URDF. Kinematic poses for moving cameras in teleoperation GS appear in HIL-GS (RA-L 2025) and Kang et al. 2026. Foveation for teleoperation appears in Tefera 2024 and Dincer 2026. Online GS for robot telepresence exists: Du et al. (RA-L 2026), GaussianNexus (UIST 2025), Tele-GS (IROS 2025) and Page et al. (IROS 2025).

What I could not find is a system that delivers per-frame, feed-forward, photoreal and temporally consistent free-viewpoint video of a changing manipulation workspace from a hybrid rig of fixed cameras plus kinematically posed moving cameras. Every live teleoperation system I found is either point clouds (Dincer 2026, GHOST 2026) or online-optimised or static GS that lags or ignores moving objects (HIL-GS at 2 Hz, Boehringer 2025, Du 2026).

The defensible claim is therefore systems-level and empirical, not a new primitive:
(a) The first geometry-guided online IBR (in the style of Ha et al.) that fuses fixed and moving cameras. Its image-space TSDF takes the kinematic robot mesh as a high-confidence input, so thin-structure and flying-pixel errors at the gripper-object contact are removed rather than merely masked. It should be evaluated with depth error and flying-pixel rate near the end effector.
(b) A controlled user study showing that temporal and geometric consistency (TCC/STED, contact-region depth error), and not only PSNR, predicts manipulation performance (success, collisions, time) against the point-cloud-plus-wrist-panel baseline of 2604.03730.
The render-and-compare mask should be presented as an adaptation of residual-based dynamic detection to the multi-camera IBR setting, not as a new insight.

Caveat: arXiv and Semantic Scholar APIs were rate-limited all session, so coverage leaned on Hugging Face paper search and Google Scholar. A concurrent 2026 arXiv paper could still be missed.
novelty.best_variant:
The cluster contains only one idea. Of its parts, the most defensible is the combination of contributions 2 and 4: robot-kinematics-as-geometry fused into the image-space TSDF and blending, measured by contact-region depth and flying-pixel error, plus a teleoperation user study that links temporal and geometric consistency of live 3D video to task success against the 2604.03730 point-cloud+wrist-RGB baseline. The hybrid-rig framing that ties them together is novel as a system, since I found no live photoreal feed-forward IBR for teleoperation that fuses fixed and robot-mounted cameras.

Contribution 1 (render-and-compare masks) is the weakest novelty claim, because ReFusion (2019) and Embodied Gaussians (2024) already establish residual-vs-rendered-model detection in real-time robotic settings. It should be positioned as an engineering generalisation.

Contribution 3 (task-aware foveation) is incremental given Tefera et al. (2024) and the 'foveated RGB detail' in Dincer et al. (2026).

A robotics or VR venue (CoRL, RSS, IEEE VR/TVCG, RA-L) is the right target. The pitch should be framed as a systems-plus-human-factors paper, not a CV-primitive paper.

sharpened.title: Robot-as-Anchor: Kinematics-Fused Online 3D Video of the Manipulation Workspace from Fixed and Wrist Cameras
sharpened.one_liner: Treat the robot as the one fully known dynamic object in the scene. Its URDF plus joint states supply exact contact-region geometry, poses for the wrist camera, and a permanent in-view registration target. Fusing these into a Ha-et-al.-style image-space TSDF gives photoreal, temporally stable free-viewpoint video of a changing workspace. That video measurably improves fine-manipulation teleoperation over the point-cloud-plus-wrist-panel interface of Dincer et al. 2026.
sharpened.core_claim: (C1, geometry) In the end-effector region (the 15 cm ball around the TCP projected into the target view), fusing (i) a kinematically posed, photometrically refined wrist RGB-D camera and (ii) the rasterised robot mesh as a high-confidence TSDF input does three things against fixed-camera-only geometry-guided IBR on held-out fixed cameras: it reduces depth error by at least 25%, reduces flying-pixel rate by at least 40%, and improves EE-crop LPIPS by at least 10%. It also beats the strong 'segment robot out and composite a URDF render' baseline on the gripper-object occlusion boundary. (C2, human factors) In a within-subject study with n≈20-24, this interface raises success on tight-clearance tasks (peg-in-hole at ≤2 mm clearance, placement into gaps) by at least 15 points and cuts collisions, compared with fused point clouds plus a floating wrist RGB panel at matched latency. Across conditions, contact-region depth error and temporal-consistency metrics (TCC/STED) predict task success better than full-frame PSNR. If C1 fails, the paper has no technical core. If C2 fails, it has no reason to exist over point clouds.
sharpened.key_insight: In teleoperation, the operator's decisions are made at the gripper-object contact. That is exactly where generic multi-view IBR is worst: thin fingers, self-occlusion, flying pixels, and fixed cameras that are far away or occluded. It is also exactly where the robot gives free, exact information: its own metric geometry at every frame, the pose of a close-range wrist camera, and a moving calibration target that is always visible. Geometry-guided IBR exposes an explicit per-pixel geometry stage (the image-space TSDF plus depth feedback), which is the natural place to inject this prior. End-to-end feed-forward Gaussians and point clouds cannot resolve robot-object visibility jointly, because they either ignore the robot or composite it afterwards. The render-and-compare motion mask is not claimed as new (ReFusion 2019, Embodied Gaussians 2024). It is the necessary adaptation that lets Ha et al.'s colour-difference temporal filter survive a moving camera.
sharpened.method: Inputs: 4-6 fixed calibrated RGB-D cameras (or stereo), 1 wrist RGB-D camera, joint states at 100+ Hz, and the URDF. (1) Wrist pose: FK pose from joint states and a hand-eye calibration, refined each frame by a 6-DoF Gauss-Newton photometric and depth alignment against the fixed-rig TSDF prediction, restricted to static-background pixels (≤3 ms, 2 pyramid levels). Fall back to FK when the residual is high. (2) Robot-aware depth: rasterise the robot mesh at the timestamp-interpolated joint state into every input view. Mark sensor-depth pixels that fall inside the dilated robot silhouette, and replace them with mesh depth at confidence w_robot and a narrow truncation, so gripper edges never produce flying pixels. Add the mesh depth as an extra 'view' input to the target-view image-space TSDF. (3) Moving-camera temporal filter: replace Ha et al.'s frame-difference gate with a residual gate M = sigmoid(a|I - Î| + b|D - D̂|), where Î and D̂ are the previous-frame TSDF rendered into the current (moving) camera pose, and the robot silhouette is always forced to 'dynamic'. Fixed cameras keep the original gate, which lets you ablate it. (4) Blend network: Ha et al.'s 4-level U-Net plus two extra input channels, the robot-mask and the per-view 'distance-to-TCP' weight. It is pretrained on DyNeRF-like multi-view data, then fine-tuned on RH20T with held-out fixed cameras as supervision. Losses are L1 + LPIPS + temporal warping loss, plus an EE-crop-weighted L1 (×4). (5) View selection: K = 4 fixed cameras chosen by pose proximity, with the wrist camera always included when the TCP is visible from the target. No foveation claim; at most a runtime ablation. (6) Display: stereo HMD via late depth-based reprojection. Robot pose is rendered at the latest joint state, which gives near-zero-latency self-motion. Budget: ≤50 ms rendering at 1280x720 on an RTX 4090 for K = 5, plus sensor latency, with end-to-end motion-to-photon measured and reported. No code exists for Ha et al., so a reimplementation (≈4-6 weeks) is required.
sharpened.why_not_engineering: The contribution is a testable claim about where the information that decides task success lives in live 3D video, and an evaluation methodology that measures it. It introduces contact-region depth error, flying-pixel rate and occlusion-boundary accuracy on held-out cameras, and links them to manipulation outcomes. It is not about a PSNR bump. The technical question is non-trivial and open: how to fuse a kinematically posed, close-range, moving camera and an exact but appearance-less mesh into a per-frame image-space TSDF without ghosting. FK error (5-15 mm on cheap arms) is on the order of the 2 cm TSDF truncation, and the robot occludes and is occluded by the manipulated object. The ablation against the 'segment and composite URDF' pipeline used by prior teleoperation systems answers a question that systems papers have assumed away. Reviewers should still expect it to read as a systems-plus-human-factors paper, and the paper should embrace that at a robotics or VR venue rather than pitch a CV primitive.
sharpened.differentiation: Dincer et al. 2026 (arXiv 2604.03730) uses the same setting: fixed RGB-D plus a wrist camera, the robot removed by YOLO and re-rendered from the URDF, foveated detail, and a 31-person study. It renders point clouds with the wrist camera as a 2D panel and has no temporal filtering. We fuse the wrist camera geometrically, resolve robot-object visibility inside the TSDF instead of by segmentation and compositing, and use their interface as the primary user-study baseline. Embodied Gaussians (arXiv 2406.10788) and ReFusion (arXiv 1905.02082): the render-vs-observe residual is theirs; we cite it and use it as a component. Their goal is state estimation or a static map, not photoreal free-viewpoint video of unmodelled objects. HIL-GS (RA-L 2025), Du et al. RA-L 2026, Wilder-Smith et al. IROS 2024 (2407.20194) and Boehringer et al. 2025 (2504.15229) use online-optimised or static GS that updates at about 2 Hz or not at all for moving objects. We are feed-forward per frame at 10-30 Hz with temporal consistency. cuMotion/nvblox masks robot pixels for collision mapping and does no rendering; we go beyond masking by inserting the mesh as geometry. GHOST 2026 (2608.29080) uses point clouds from onboard cameras only. Tefera 2024 and Dincer 2026 already use foveation, so we drop it as a contribution. Ha et al. (CVPR 2025) assume a static rig and generic scenes, and their own ablation shows TSDF guidance barely moves PSNR (31.16 to 31.17). We argue its value appears in contact-region geometry and consistency, and test that claim directly.

datasets: RH20T (https://rh20t.github.io/, arXiv 2307.00595): 8-10 fixed global RGB-D cameras plus 1-2 in-hand cameras, 1280x720 at 10 Hz, intrinsics and extrinsics, joint angles and gripper pose provided. This is the primary public benchmark: hold out 1-2 fixed cameras as ground truth while the wrist camera moves. Caveats: 10 Hz, software-timestamp sync, and RealSense depth noise on thin or dark objects.
DROID (named in the cluster file; availability not re-verified this session): 2 external stereo cameras plus 1 wrist camera, a sparse stress test for generalisation only.
DyNeRF / Neural 3D Video and D3DMV (the base paper's benchmarks): used only to confirm the reimplementation of Ha et al. reaches reported numbers (±0.5 dB), not for the claim.

Custom capture (required): a tabletop arm (Franka, xArm or UR) with 4-6 hardware-synced RGB-D or stereo cameras at 30 Hz, a wrist D405-class camera, and a 7th held-out camera. It is needed for 30 Hz evaluation and thin-object tasks (cables, pegs, transparent-free objects), and is the only way to run the closed-loop user study.

experiments.capture_notes: Public RH20T covers the offline NVS claim (C1) at 10 Hz. The user-study claim (C2) and any 30 Hz or thin-object evaluation need your own rig. That rig needs one arm with a stable URDF and hand-eye calibration, 4-6 hardware-synced RGB-D or stereo cameras (RealSense D4xx or ZED X with a genlock or trigger cable), a wrist D405, one extra held-out camera, and a Quest 3 or Vision Pro HMD. Budget roughly USD 5-15k if the arm is borrowed from a robotics lab. Without access to a robot arm, drop the project.

review.kill_criteria:
Stop or pivot if any of the following holds.
(1) On RH20T, adding the robot mesh gives less than 15% relative reduction in EE-region depth error or flying-pixel rate over fixed-only. Also stop if it is statistically indistinguishable from segment-and-composite: then the prior is fully captured by the trivial pipeline prior systems already use.
(2) FK plus refinement leaves the wrist-camera pose error above about 1 cm, so the wrist view ghosts and adding it worsens EE-crop LPIPS relative to fixed-only. The moving-camera story then collapses back to a 2D wrist panel.
(3) A pilot user study (n = 6-8, one peg-in-hole task) shows less than a 10-point success difference and no time or collision difference against point cloud plus wrist panel at matched latency. If photoreal IBR does not change operator behaviour, the significance argument is gone.
(4) A concurrent paper appears with feed-forward, per-frame photoreal IBR fusing fixed and wrist cameras with robot geometry for teleoperation. Re-run the arXiv search monthly; the APIs were rate-limited in both novelty passes.
(5) No robot-lab partner is secured within 1 month.

reviewer_objections.objection: This is systems integration of known pieces: ReFusion or Embodied Gaussians residual masks, cuMotion robot filtering, and Ha et al. IBR. There is no new primitive.
reviewer_objections.rebuttal: Agreed on the pieces, and the paper says so explicitly. The contribution is the empirical finding and the metric: contact-region geometry and temporal consistency, not PSNR, determine teleoperation outcomes. Kinematic fusion inside the per-frame geometry stage measurably beats the segment-and-composite design that every prior teleoperation system uses. Target a robotics or VR venue where validated system-plus-human-factors contributions are first-class, and include the FK-error sweep, which characterises when fusion helps.

reviewer_objections.objection: Why not just render the robot from its URDF (as Dincer et al. and Boehringer et al. do) and spend effort on the scene?
reviewer_objections.rebuttal: The segment-and-composite baseline is included and evaluated at the occlusion boundary. Compositing resolves robot-versus-scene depth order per pixel from noisy sensor depth, so fingers visually penetrate or float above objects at contact, which is exactly the judgement operators need. Fusing mesh depth into the TSDF also stops robot flying pixels from corrupting the object's depth. If this baseline ties, the kill criterion fires. The study is designed to be able to lose.

reviewer_objections.objection: Point clouds are good enough. User studies show operators adapt, and photorealism is a luxury that costs latency.
reviewer_objections.rebuttal: The within-subject study matches latency across interfaces, crosses interface with a 0/150 ms latency factor, and reports motion-to-photon for both. Tasks are chosen where depth ordering at millimetre clearance matters (peg-in-hole at ≤2 mm, placement into gaps, cable routing). The mixed-effects analysis tests whether the rendering metrics predict success, so a null result is itself a publishable, informative finding for the IBR community.

reviewer_objections.objection: The RH20T evaluation is weak. It runs at 10 Hz with software sync and noisy RealSense 'ground truth' depth near thin grippers.
reviewer_objections.rebuttal: On robot pixels, the ground truth is the exact mesh depth, which is noise-free. Object pixels use held-out sensor depth with a validity mask plus an occlusion-boundary F-score from SAM2 masks. The custom 30 Hz, hardware-synced rig with a dedicated held-out camera is the primary quantitative benchmark, and RH20T demonstrates that the result generalises to a public dataset.

reviewer_objections.objection: Generalisation and deployment: the blend network is fine-tuned per rig, FK and hand-eye error on cheap arms is large, and the base method has no public code.
reviewer_objections.rebuttal: The FK-error sweep and the photometric refinement quantify robustness explicitly. The blend network is trained on RH20T and tested zero-shot on the custom rig (different cameras and robot) to report cross-rig transfer. The reimplementation of Ha et al. is released and validated against their DyNeRF numbers, itself a community contribution given that no official code exists.

effort.months: 8-10 (about 1.5 months for reimplementation and validation of Ha et al., 1 month for the RH20T C1 study, 2 months for rig build and calibration, 2 months for the fused system, runtime and HMD, 1.5 months for the IRB and user study, and 1 month for writing). Cutting to C1 plus a small pilot gives a workshop or RA-L-letter version in about 5 months.
effort.people: 2: one vision/graphics PhD student (IBR, TSDF, blend network) plus one robotics student or collaborator (arm, hand-eye calibration, teleop stack, user study). Access to a robotics lab is mandatory.
effort.compute: 2-4 consumer or workstation GPUs (RTX 4090/A6000 class) for blend-net fine-tuning (days, not weeks); 1 RTX 4090 for live rendering. Hardware: borrowed arm, 5-7 RGB-D or stereo cameras with trigger sync, a wrist D405, and a Quest 3; about USD 5-15k excluding the arm.

review.venue: Primary: CoRL 2027 (deadline around mid-2027) or IEEE RA-L with an ICRA/IROS presentation, both rolling or mid-2027, framed as a teleoperation interface plus a human-factors finding. Secondary: IEEE VR 2028 / TVCG or ISMAR 2027 if the user study is the strongest part. Do not target CVPR/ICCV: the CV-primitive novelty is too thin, and reviewers there will read it as engineering. RSS 2027 (early 2027 deadline) and IEEE VR 2027 are too soon given the missing base code and rig.
review.synergies: (1) Latency and predictive display: the robot is the one object whose future is known from commanded joint trajectories. Rendering the robot mesh at the commanded pose in the same TSDF gives a principled predictive display, pairing with forecasting and latency-compensation directions. (2) Self-calibration: the always-visible robot mesh yields a continuous render-and-compare signal to detect and correct extrinsic drift of the fixed cameras. This pairs with calibration-free or unposed-rig telepresence directions (for example Tele360-style LM refinement); keep it to an ablation here, since robot-based camera calibration has prior art. (3) Learned depth front-ends: robot-mesh depth is free metric supervision for online adaptation of stereo or monocular depth models, pairing with temporally consistent stereo directions such as PPMStereo-type memory stereo. (4) Consistency-aware metrics: the contact-region and TCC-predicts-task-success analysis generalises to human telepresence (gaze and hand-contact regions), pairing with the perceptual and temporal-metric direction. (5) Bandwidth: a paper series could add ROI-prioritised streaming (a wrist-camera and EE-region bitrate budget) as a follow-up, pairing with compression and streaming directions for the base pipeline. (6) Moving-camera telepresence generally: the render-and-compare gate transfers to HMD-mounted or handheld cameras in human telepresence rigs.

cited_work_check.title: Cloak of Invisibility: Real-Time Privacy-Preserving Volumetric Video Streaming (InViStream)
cited_work_check.note: Khalili et al. (UCLA and Nokia Bell Labs), Aug 2026. Confirmed from the HTML full text. Removed points are set to (inf,inf,inf) and deleted before cloud fusion. There is no fill or inpainting, no novel-view rendering and no background memory. Leakage is measured as the Private-Object Detection Rate (PODR) at 6.3% on synthetic data and 14.3% on real data. threats.title: An Efficient Diminished Reality Approach Using Real-Time Surface Reconstruction
threats.what_overlaps: This is exactly the core mechanism. An on-the-fly dense 3D reconstruction stored in a voxel grid (TSDF-style) is used to render the background into the region of a removed 3D object, and inpainting is used only for the remaining unobserved holes. The paper frames this as better than inpainting for non-planar scenes. 'Retrieval plus reprojection from a voxel-anchored memory, with a generative fallback' is therefore not a new insight.
threats.what_remains_different: It uses a single moving AR camera and renders only the capturing camera's own view. It removes static objects only. There are no remote free viewpoints, no fixed multi-camera rig, no dynamic or person removal, no privacy leakage criterion and no edit propagation.

threats.title: Online Adaptive Integration of Observation and Inpainting for Diminished Reality with Online Surface Reconstruction
threats.what_overlaps: The paper states the observation-based vs inpainting-based dichotomy explicitly. It fills the region of interest first by inpainting and then progressively with observed colour and shape from an RGB-D SLAM surface reconstruction as observations accumulate. This is the 'observed history first, hallucination only for never-seen pixels' idea, with online adaptive switching.
threats.what_remains_different: It uses a single moving camera and its own-view AR output. There is no multi-view rig, no novel-view 3D video, no privacy objective and no dynamic scene or people.

threats.title: InpaintFusion: Incremental RGB-D Inpainting for 3D Scenes
threats.what_overlaps: This is real-time DR in which inpainted colour and depth are fused into a global surfel map through RGB-D SLAM and then projected back for rendering. The fill is therefore anchored in 3D and stays consistent as the viewpoint changes, which is the 'view-consistent by construction via a 3D-anchored fill' argument.
threats.what_remains_different: The fill is inpainted (hallucinated), not retrieved from observed history. It uses a single handheld camera, and there is no privacy objective, no multi-view free-viewpoint video and no dynamic content.

threats.title: Observation-based diminished reality: a systematic literature review
threats.what_overlaps: A survey of 67 key papers from 2000 to 2024 on DR that fills from real background observations (multi-view, pre-recorded or accumulated). It shows that 'authentic fill from observed data instead of hallucination' is an established DR sub-field, and any novelty claim framed around it will be rejected by ISMAR/IEEE VR reviewers.
threats.what_remains_different: It is a survey. By its scope, the reviewed work targets AR see-through for the capturing user's own view, not live multi-view 3D video rendered to remote free viewpoints.

threats.title: Mobile Diminished Reality for Preserving 3D Visual Privacy / Utility-Privacy Aware Mobile DR Framework for 3D Visual Privacy / AI-Enhanced Mobile DR for Preserving 3D Visual Privacy (Tabet, Kayssi, Elhajj)
threats.what_overlaps: A real-time DR framework designed to hide private 3D objects in live MR feeds and to stay effective during 3D rotation around the sensitive object. It reports PSNR plus privacy metrics above 90%, and the TPS-ISA version adds a privacy-utility trade-off metric under free camera motion. 'Privacy removal that survives viewpoint change' plus a privacy metric is therefore already published for mobile MR.
threats.what_remains_different: The fill uses 2D inpainting with optical-flow tracking on a single mobile camera. There is no observed-history fill, no multi-camera rig, no rendering of novel views for remote viewers and no geometric or depth leakage criterion.

threats.title: Efficient 3D Reconstruction, Streaming and Visualization of Static and Dynamic Scene Parts for Multi-client Live-telepresence in Large-scale Environments
threats.what_overlaps: A live telepresence system that keeps a persistent voxel (TSDF) model of static content with semantics and instances, alongside separately streamed dynamic point clouds. Instance-level static/dynamic separation and a persistent voxel memory of the observed static scene for remote VR viewing are both here. Dropping a dynamic instance's stream and showing the voxel memory behind it is close to trivial on top of this.
threats.what_remains_different: There is no removal, privacy or editing objective. It uses a single moving RGB-D camera, not a fixed synced rig with IBR blending. There is no fill-fidelity or leakage evaluation.

threats.title: DimSplat: A Real-Time Diminished Reality System for Revisiting Environments Using Gaussian Splats in Mobile WebXR
threats.what_overlaps: Uses a Gaussian-splat reconstruction of a previously captured environment state to remove objects in real time (60 FPS), i.e. 'fill from observed earlier state' with a modern 3D representation.
threats.what_remains_different: The background is pre-captured and static, and the target is mobile AR. There is no live multi-view capture, no dynamic people, no privacy objective and no remote novel views.

threats.title: Remove360: Benchmarking Residuals After Object Removal in 3D Gaussian Splatting
threats.what_overlaps: Benchmarks semantic residuals and leakage after 3D object removal, using real post-removal ground-truth captures. The benchmark design (capture after physical removal) and the leakage-measurement angle overlap with the proposed benchmark and leakage audit.
threats.what_remains_different: Static, offline 3DGS. There is no live video, no people and no telepresence.

threats.title: Cloak of Invisibility / InViStream
threats.what_overlaps: Real-time privacy-from-source for multi-view RGB-D volumetric streaming, with depth-aware masking, cross-view propagation of privacy decisions and a silhouette-leakage metric (PODR). This is the privacy half of the idea in the same multi-camera RGB-D setting.
threats.what_remains_different: No fill (holes remain), no background memory, no novel-view rendering or view-dependent leakage evaluation, no edits, and captures are sequential and static rather than synced live video.

threats.title: Preserve, Reveal, Expand: Faithful 4D Video Editing with Region-Aware Conditioning (PREX)
threats.what_overlaps: 4D editing that explicitly separates 'reveal' (disoccluded) regions and fills them with observation-backed appearance cues rather than pure generation.
threats.what_remains_different: Generative and offline. It has no live rig, no privacy objective and no TSDF memory.
