novelty.remaining_novel_angle:
The stated key insight is not novel. Filling a removed region by re-rendering an online voxel or TSDF reconstruction of what was observed earlier, and using inpainting only for never-observed pixels, is classic observation-based diminished reality: Kunert et al. CW 2019 (voxel grid plus inpainting fallback), Kato et al. ISMAR-Adj 2022 (adaptive observation/inpainting with online RGB-D SLAM surfaces), InpaintFusion TVCG 2020, a 2024 systematic review of the sub-field, and DimSplat VRW 2025 with Gaussian splats. Privacy-motivated 3D DR that survives viewpoint rotation, with privacy metrics, also exists (Tabet et al. 2023/2024). Privacy-from-source for multi-view RGB-D volumetric streaming exists as well (InViStream 2026).

What remains defensible is the setting shift and what it forces technically. (1) The DR output is not the capturing camera's own view but arbitrary remote novel views synthesized live from a fixed synced multi-camera rig. Removal must therefore happen in geometry before image-based fusion and blending, covering per-view Gaussians, TSDF depth inputs and the blend network's background prediction, so the removed instance cannot reappear through another camera's pixels, through depth silhouettes, or through the learned background image. (2) A view-agnostic, geometric leakage criterion and audit (no rendered novel view may contain surfaces of the removed instance), evaluated along novel-view trajectories for dynamic people. InViStream only measures detector-based PODR on source views, and Remove360 is static and offline. (3) An observed-history background memory for a fixed rig in which people move and objects arrive, with timestamped and confidence-gated updates driven by the base paper's static masks, evaluated for fill fidelity against empty-scene ground truth. This is a capture protocol and benchmark that live multi-view DR lacks.

Live surface-anchored edit propagation is a weaker, incremental add-on. Offline 4D editing is crowded, and colour and sticker edits on TSDF surfaces are engineering. The paper must cite and position against the observation-based DR literature and must not claim 'retrieval instead of hallucination' as the insight. The contribution is multi-view, free-viewpoint, dynamic, leakage-certified DR for live 3D telepresence.
novelty.best_variant: There is only one idea in the cluster. Its most defensible core is contribution 2 (geometry-level removal before IBR fusion, with a formal novel-view leakage criterion and audit) combined with contribution 4 (the empty-scene ground-truth capture protocol and benchmark for live multi-view removal). Together they are what separates this work from both InViStream (source-side holes, detector-based leakage, no novel views) and classic observation-based DR (single-camera own-view AR). The TSDF-anchored background memory (contribution 1) should be presented as the adaptation of known observation-based DR to a fixed multi-camera rig with moving people, not as the key insight. Edit propagation (contribution 3) should be dropped or scoped as a demo.

sharpened.title: Leak-Proof Diminished Reality for Live Free-Viewpoint 3D Video: Removing People Before Fusion and Filling from Observed History
sharpened.one_liner: In live image-based 3D video from a fixed rig, a removed person can reappear at a novel view through several routes. These are other cameras' pixels, depth silhouettes, previous-frame depth feedback, the learned background image and the shape of the fill region. We remove the person in 3D with a fail-closed rule before fusion, fill the region from a TSDF-anchored memory of what the rig actually saw, and certify the result against an attacker suite along novel-view trajectories.
sharpened.core_claim: Setting: live geometry-guided image-based rendering (IBR) from a fixed synced rig. Claim (a): per-view 2D removal still leaks the removed person at held-out and novel views. This covers leaving holes (InViStream-style) and 2D video inpainting of the rendered view (ProPainter-class). An attacker that recovers the silhouette gets mask IoU of at least 0.4, and a pose estimator recovers at least 50% of keypoints. Claim (b): fail-closed removal by 3D consensus before fusion, plus the previous-frame feedback reset, plus fill from observed history cuts those attacker scores to within 0.05 of the same attacker's false-positive rate on renders of the empty scene. Claim (c): inside the removed region, fill from observed history beats the best real-time 2D inpainting by at least 2 dB PSNR and at least 0.05 LPIPS against empty-scene ground truth, and has better TCC/STED. Claim (d): all of this adds at most 10 ms/frame on top of the base pipeline. The claim is falsified if hole-leaving or 2D inpainting already reaches control-level attacker scores, or if the memory fill is not measurably better than real-time inpainting where the background was observed.
sharpened.key_insight: Retrieval instead of hallucination is not the insight. That belongs to observation-based diminished reality (DR): Kunert et al. CW 2019, Kato et al. ISMAR-Adj 2022, and the 2024 review. The new point is that multi-view geometry-guided IBR is a leaky sink, and removal has to be enforced at the fusion layer, not in any one image. In the base paper's pipeline a removed instance can come back through five routes. (1) Cross-view pixels: any of the K views whose mask missed the person still supplies its splatted Gaussians. (2) Depth: TSDF inputs shape the fused surface, and so the silhouette. (3) Temporal feedback: the previous-frame novel-view depth is fused back in, which carries removed geometry forward. (4) Learned background: I_BG is predicted from context. (5) Negative space: the outline of a hole, or of a hallucinated fill, shows the silhouette and pose to an attacker. Route 5 ties privacy to fill fidelity. Only a fill that matches the true background closes that route, and a fixed rig can supply one, because each surface point was usually seen by another camera now or by any camera earlier. So in this setting authentic fill is a privacy mechanism, not only a cosmetic one.
sharpened.method:
Base: reimplement the base paper's pipeline (per-view opaque pixel Gaussians, image-based TSDF with previous-frame depth feedback, 4-level U-Net blend). There is no public code. Where time is short, use a simpler depth-weighted blend.

(1) Fail-closed 3D-consensus instance masks.
- Per camera: a lightweight instance segmenter with temporal propagation (YOLO-seg or EfficientSAM-class plus a mask tracker) runs at the sender in parallel across cameras.
- Masked pixels are lifted with depth into a coarse voxel grid (about 2 cm) and voted there.
- A voxel is private if ANY camera votes for it with confidence above c_low (fail-closed). The hull is dilated in 3D by delta = 3 cm, not in 2D.
- The hull is reprojected into all K views to give union masks. This fixes routes 1 and 2 even when one view's 2D mask misses.

(2) Removal at every IBR input.
- Drop the Gaussians inside the union mask.
- Set TSDF weight omega_k = 0 inside it, so a hole cannot carve a silhouette-shaped depth void. Replace with memory depth.
- Reset omega_tmp in the reprojected hull region, so the previous-frame depth feedback cannot carry removed geometry forward (route 3).
- Override the blend network's background image I_BG and weight w_BG in the removed region with the memory render (route 4).
- Fine-tune the U-Net with an extra 'removed-region' channel and a boundary-seam loss.

(3) Observed-history background memory.
- Per camera, a background plate: RGB, depth, confidence and last-seen time.
- A pixel updates only when all of these hold: the base paper's static mask says static, the pixel is outside every private or dynamic instance, it is depth-consistent over at least N frames, and it is 'farther-or-equal' to the current plate depth (a background-modelling rule).
- A slow EMA on colour absorbs lighting drift.
- To produce a fill, render the plates through the same forward-splat and TSDF path into the target view: current other-camera pixels first (spatial history), then older plates (temporal history).
- Photometric harmonisation: fit a per-frame affine colour model on a static ring around the region and apply it to the memory render.
- Pixels never observed (confidence 0) fall back to the U-Net background image or a one-step fixer. They are flagged and counted.
- Privacy of the memory itself: private instances are never written to plates, and a time-to-live (TTL) plus a purge API bound retention.

(4) Attacker-based leakage audit (the evaluation contribution).
- Along held-out-camera and interpolated novel-view trajectories, run five checks:
  - (a) person or object detector recall (PODR-comparable);
  - (b) a silhouette-recovery attacker, i.e. an inpainting-forensics or segmentation network fine-tuned to localise filled regions, scored by IoU with the true silhouette;
  - (c) 2D pose-keypoint recovery;
  - (d) person re-ID similarity to the removed identity;
  - (e) a geometric residual: rendered depth within tau of the removed instance's last-known surface.
- Every score is reported relative to the same attacker run on empty-scene control renders.

No generative model on the critical path. Budget: segmentation 5-8 ms per camera in parallel at the sender, voxel voting and reprojection about 2 ms, memory render about 3-5 ms (reusing the splat path). Target overhead is at most 10 ms, keeping the pipeline at 40-60 ms/frame on one RTX 4090.
sharpened.why_not_engineering: The paper makes three claims beyond a system. (i) It identifies and measures the leakage routes that are specific to multi-view geometry-guided IBR. Reviewers can falsify this: we show that obvious baselines (per-view masking with holes, and 2D inpainting on the rendered view) leak at novel views, and ablate each route. (ii) It shows that fill fidelity and privacy are coupled through the shape of the removed region: the attacker's silhouette IoU falls with fill PSNR, and hole-leaving is the worst case. So the observation-based fill is justified by a privacy objective, not by looks. (iii) It contributes an attacker-based certification protocol and an empty-scene ground-truth benchmark for live multi-view removal, which the field lacks. InViStream measures detector PODR on source views only. Remove360 is static and offline. The observation-based DR literature evaluates the capturing camera's own view. The mechanisms themselves (voxel voting, plates, masking) are deliberately simple; the contribution is the problem formulation, the evidence of leakage and the certification.
sharpened.differentiation:
- Observation-based DR (Kunert CW 2019; Kato ISMAR-Adj 2022; InpaintFusion TVCG 2020; the Eskandari 2024 review; DimSplat VRW 2025): single moving camera, output only to the camera's own view, mostly static objects, no privacy criterion. We cite them as the source of 'fill from observations' and do not claim it. Our delta: a fixed multi-camera rig rendering arbitrary remote novel views, dynamic people, removal enforced before multi-view fusion, and leakage certification.
- InViStream (arXiv 2608.11645): multi-view RGB-D privacy-from-source. It leaves holes, has no novel-view rendering or background memory, and uses detector PODR on sequential static captures. We show quantitatively that its holes leak silhouette and pose to an attacker at novel views, and that authentic fill closes that route.
- Tabet et al. mobile DR privacy (iMETA 2023, TPS-ISA 2024): 2D inpainting plus optical flow on one mobile camera. Their privacy metric is detector-style. Ours adds geometric, silhouette and pose attackers under multi-view novel views.
- The Efficient 3D Reconstruction... Live-Telepresence paper (ICCVW 2023, arXiv 2211.14310): persistent static voxel memory, but no removal objective and no leakage evaluation. We treat it as evidence that the memory is standard.
- NSTM (arXiv 2607.15271): long-horizon memory for occlusions, with no removal or privacy objective. It could serve as an alternative memory backend in an ablation.
- Offline 4D editing (Dynamic-eDiTor, EditCast3D, 4D-MoDe, PREX): edit propagation is dropped from the paper, apart from one demo figure.

datasets: DyNeRF / Neural 3D Video (public; 18-21 static GoPro cameras): background scenes for the synthetic-insertion benchmark. A 3D human sequence (4K4D-, THuman- or DNA-Rendering-style mesh) is composited in with a depth z-test, which gives exact ground truth for fill and leakage. Caveat: the cook barely moves, so real removal of the cook has no observable background and is used only for the coverage and fallback analysis.

ENeRF-Outdoor (18 synced cameras; access by agreement, verified on the ENeRF repo page): several people walking in a fixed outdoor rig. Used for removing a real person with the attacker metrics, which need no background ground truth, and for fill evaluation only on pixels whose ground truth exists in frames where the person is elsewhere (with a disjoint temporal split from the memory-building frames).
D3DMV (base paper's third dataset): a cross-dataset check of the full pipeline.

CMU Panoptic Studio (public; HD cameras plus Kinect RGB-D; multi-person social sequences): removing a bystander in multi-person scenes with the attacker metrics. Verify that the Kinect depth is synced before relying on it.
Remove360 (arXiv 2508.11431): not used as training data. Its capture-after-physical-removal protocol is adopted and cited.

CUSTOM (required): 6-8 synced RGB-D cameras (Orbbec Femto Bolt / ZED-class stereo) in 3-4 rooms (office, living room, a meeting room with windows for lighting drift). Each room has empty-scene plates, sequences with 1-3 people entering, sitting and leaving, and objects placed and then physically removed. That gives 10-15 sequences of 2-5 min each, with 2 held-out cameras per room for ground truth. This is the benchmark contribution. Publish it under consent forms.
baselines: Base pipeline with no removal (upper bound on leakage).
InViStream-style per-view masking before fusion that leaves holes: blend net and I_BG fill naturally.
Per-view 2D masking plus real-time 2D video inpainting of the rendered novel view (ProPainter-class; E2FGVI as a faster option).
Per-view masking plus a one-step diffusion fixer on the rendered view (Difix3D+ or NVIDIA Fixer): a generative fill, not real-time-comparable, used for a quality reference.
Masking of the source views plus 2D video inpainting of each source view before fusion (MiniMax-Remover-class, offline), which tests cross-view consistency.
Observation-based DR adapted naively: a single-camera Kato/Kunert-style memory used per camera, with no 3D consensus and no feedback reset.
Offline upper bound: per-scene 4DGS trained on only the non-private pixels (or Dynamic-eDiTor-style removal), for quality only.
metrics: Fill fidelity in the removed region against empty-scene or composite ground truth: PSNR, SSIM and LPIPS; full-frame PSNR as well.

Leakage, each relative to the same attacker on empty-scene control renders, along held-out-camera and interpolated novel-view trajectories: detector recall (PODR-comparable); silhouette-recovery attacker IoU; 2D pose keypoint recovery rate (PCK); re-ID cosine similarity and rank-1 against a gallery; geometric residual (fraction of rendered depth pixels within tau of the removed instance's surface).
Worst-case leakage over the trajectory (max per sequence), not only the mean. Report the leakage-free frame rate.
Temporal: TCC, STED and flicker in the removed region; view consistency (SDV / MEt3R).
Coverage: the fraction of removed pixels filled from observation versus the fallback, as a function of time since the person entered.
Latency breakdown (segmentation, voting, memory render, blend) on a stated GPU. Memory footprint.
Robustness curves: leakage versus injected segmentation noise (missed views, 2D mask erosion of 1-10 px, dropped frames).
User study (n of about 20): naturalness MOS, plus a forced-choice 'was someone removed here / where' test (privacy as perceived by humans).
key_ablations: Close the leakage routes one at a time: without 3D-consensus union masks (per-view masks only), without depth masking (omega_k kept), without the previous-frame feedback reset, without the I_BG override, and without memory fill (holes). Each is measured by attacker IoU, PCK and re-ID.
Fill source: spatial only (current other cameras), temporal only (history), both, and generative fallback only.
Fail-closed versus majority-vote consensus, and the 3D dilation delta: the trade-off between leakage and over-removal (false removal of the telepresence user).
Harmonisation on or off, under lighting drift (window sequences).
Memory update rule: farther-or-equal versus plain EMA versus the base paper's difference mask only (does memory get polluted by slow-moving people?).
Attacker strength: an off-the-shelf detector versus an attacker fine-tuned on our fills (adaptive adversary).
experiments.capture_notes: Public multi-view dynamic datasets lack empty-scene ground truth behind removed people. Studio human datasets (DNA-Rendering, ENeRF-Outdoor) do not document background plates; this was checked on their pages and they are not mentioned. Public data therefore supports (a) synthetic 3D human insertion into DyNeRF with exact ground truth, and (b) attacker-only leakage evaluation on ENeRF-Outdoor and Panoptic. A small custom rig (6-8 RGB-D or stereo cameras, about $3-6k, hardware sync, one weekend of calibration) is needed for the real-world fill-fidelity benchmark, with physical-removal ground truth (Remove360 protocol) and realistic shadows and lighting. Budget 3-4 weeks for the rig and 2 weeks for capture and annotation. Obtain informed consent and an IRB exemption for participants, since the benchmark itself contains identifiable people. Release only with consent, and blur faces in any non-benchmark footage.

review.first_two_week_test:
Composite-insertion test on DyNeRF with a minimal reimplementation. The base paper's code is not released, so build a stripped version: per-view forward-splat with gsplat, depth-weighted blending, the image-based TSDF with the previous-frame feedback, no U-Net, and RAFT-Stereo depth.

Days 1-4:
- Composite a walking 3D human (a rendered mesh sequence with depth) into 2 DyNeRF scenes over 100 frames, using a z-test against the stereo depth.
- The original frames are exact ground truth for the fill and for leakage.
- Generate masks from the known composite, corrupted with realistic noise: 1 of K views missed on 10% of frames, and 3 px erosion.

Days 5-10: compare four variants.
- (A) Per-view masking with holes.
- (B) (A) plus ProPainter on the rendered held-out view.
- (C) 3D-consensus fail-closed union masks plus the feedback reset, still with holes.
- (D) (C) plus memory fill (per-camera plates with the farther-or-equal rule, rendered through the same splat path).

Days 11-14: measure, on the 9 held-out cameras plus 2 interpolated trajectories:
- PSNR and LPIPS in the removed region;
- silhouette-attacker IoU, using SAM2 or a person segmenter plus a simple inpainting-forensics localiser (e.g. an off-the-shelf IML model);
- PCK of a 2D pose estimator;
- all scores against empty-scene control renders.

What counts as validation:
- (A) and (B) both leak (IoU at least 0.4 or PCK at least 50%);
- (C) removes cross-view and feedback leakage (the detector recall drop is visible);
- (D) brings the attacker to within 0.05 of control and beats (B) by at least 2 dB in the region.

A single pass through this setup also produces the headline leakage figure for the paper.
review.kill_criteria:
Kill or pivot if any of these hold after the 2-week test and the first custom capture.
(1) Simple baselines already reach control-level attacker scores at novel views: 2D inpainting on the rendered view gets silhouette IoU and PCK within 0.05 of control. Then there is no leakage problem to solve, and the paper reduces to a quality comparison already covered by observation-based DR.
(2) The memory fill does not beat real-time 2D video inpainting by at least 1 dB PSNR or 0.03 LPIPS in removed regions where the background was observed.
(3) On realistic room sequences, the observed coverage of removed regions is below about 60% after 10 s, so most pixels fall back to hallucination and the authenticity argument collapses.
(4) Segmentation errors dominate: with realistic real-time masks, leakage stays above 2x control even with fail-closed 3D consensus, or fail-closed over-removal wipes out the telepresence user more than 5% of the time.
(5) A new 2026 paper appears that does live multi-view free-viewpoint removal with novel-view leakage evaluation. Re-check arXiv monthly, with alerts on InViStream follow-ups and on NSTM.

reviewer_objections.objection: This is observation-based diminished reality (Kunert 2019, Kato 2022, InpaintFusion, DimSplat) moved onto a multi-camera rig. The memory, voxel voting and masking are standard, so this is a systems paper.
reviewer_objections.rebuttal: We agree the fill mechanism is known, and we cite it as such. The contribution is the problem and the evidence. Multi-view IBR has leakage routes that do not exist in single-camera own-view DR: cross-view pixels, the depth silhouette in the TSDF, previous-frame depth feedback, the learned background and the outline of the removed region. We show that natural baselines leak at novel views, with route-by-route ablations. We also show that fill fidelity is causally tied to privacy through that outline, and we release an attacker-based certification protocol plus an empty-scene ground-truth benchmark. None of this exists for live free-viewpoint video.

reviewer_objections.objection: The guarantee is only as good as the segmenter. One missed frame and the person is back, so 'leak-proof' overclaims.
reviewer_objections.rebuttal: The claim is conditional and measured, not absolute. Fail-closed 3D consensus means a person must be missed by all K cameras at once to leak. We report leakage against injected mask noise (missed views, erosion, dropped frames) and the worst case per trajectory, not only means. We also report the cost of over-removal. The title and claims will say 'certified against an attacker suite', not 'guaranteed'.

reviewer_objections.objection: Observed history only helps when things move. The background behind a static private object, or a seated person, was never observed, so you are back to hallucination.
reviewer_objections.rebuttal: There are two sources of coverage. Other rig cameras see around the occluder now (spatial coverage), and past frames see behind people who move (temporal coverage). We report coverage over time and flag the fallback pixels honestly. For deployment, an empty-room enrollment scan (as in booth systems such as Starline) supplies plates for static private objects. The DyNeRF cook case is included explicitly as a failure mode.

reviewer_objections.objection: The ground truth is weak. Synthetic insertion lacks real shadows, reflections and lighting interaction, and public real datasets have no ground truth behind people.
reviewer_objections.rebuttal: That is why we build the custom benchmark with physical-removal and empty-scene ground truth (Remove360 protocol), including windowed rooms with lighting drift. Shadow and reflection residue is measured as its own leakage route, with an EffectErase-style effect-removal baseline as a discussion point. Synthetic insertion is used only for controlled ablations with exact ground truth.

reviewer_objections.objection: InViStream already does real-time privacy-from-source for multi-view RGB-D. Leaving holes is safe enough, and filling adds a risk of stale memory showing past private states.
reviewer_objections.rebuttal: We show quantitatively that holes are not safe at novel views: the outline of a hole leaks silhouette and pose to an attacker, and our fill closes that route. Stale-memory risk is handled by design. Private instances are never written to plates, and there is a TTL and a purge API. We also evaluate a memory-poisoning case: an object shown once, then removed, must not reappear.

effort.months: 6-8 (2 weeks feasibility test; 2 months pipeline reimplementation plus removal and memory; 1.5 months rig build and capture; 2 months evaluation, attacker suite and user study; 1 month writing)
effort.people: 1 PhD student full-time plus 1 part-time (capture, user study, IRB)
effort.compute: 1-2 RTX 4090/A6000-class GPUs. Training is limited to fine-tuning the blend U-Net with a removed-region channel (about 1-2 GPU-days) and fine-tuning the attacker models. About $3-6k of hardware for 6-8 synced RGB-D or stereo cameras.

review.venue: ISMAR 2027 (TVCG journal track) as the primary target: the diminished-reality and privacy community values the leakage and certification framing and the benchmark. Fallback is IEEE VR 2028 (TVCG). CVPR/ICCV is a stretch unless the attacker and benchmark contribution is unusually strong. A CVPR 2027 workshop paper (e.g. on privacy or XR) is a reasonable early marker for the synthetic-insertion results.
review.synergies:
- Long-horizon memory for disocclusion: the same TSDF-anchored background plates fill ordinary disocclusions around the telepresence user, fixing the base paper's per-frame I_BG. This work could be a shared memory module across two papers, or a combined 'observed-history memory for live IBR' paper, where removal is one use case.
- Bandwidth and streaming: sender-side removal plus a background plate sent once, with only foreground and instance deltas streamed, gives privacy-by-design and compression together (compare 4D-MoDe, MetaStream).
- Semantic static/dynamic separation: the instance masks and 3D voting replace the base paper's fragile colour-difference static masks, improving temporal depth filtering under lighting changes and flames.
- One-step or causal generative disocclusion (Difix3D+/Fixer, InstantViR, Bonn's real-time inpainting transformer): the natural fallback for never-observed pixels, with the attacker suite as an evaluation lens for hallucination.
- Temporal consistency and evaluation benchmarks: the empty-scene ground-truth capture protocol and worst-case-over-trajectory metrics extend to any live 3D video quality study.
- Relighting and colour harmonisation across cameras: the harmonisation step is shared.
- Trust and authenticity in telepresence (VoluMe-style 'authenticity' arguments): the flagged fallback-pixel map is a provenance signal, which could become a paper on verifiable, provenance-tagged 3D video.

name: Error-propagation theory of when geometry-guided IBR beats learned renderers (bias/variance, flicker)

cited_work_check.title: Geometry-guided Online 3D Video Synthesis with Multi-View Temporal Consistency (Ha et al., CVPR 2025)
cited_work_check.note: Exists, and the authors and abstract match. The ablation numbers the ideator relies on (PSNR 31.16 vs 31.17, STED 95.4 to 68.8) come from the local deepread.md. The deep read also records that TCC barely moves (0.869 to 0.872) and that the ablation is a single DyNeRF run. So the 'puzzle' rests on one unreplicated run, and only STED shows it clearly.

cited_work_check.title: LVSM: A Large View Synthesis Model with Minimal 3D Inductive Bias (ICLR 2025)
cited_work_check.note: Confirmed. It is a geometry-free transformer, 1.5-3.5 dB above prior SOTA on static benchmarks, with no temporal or error-theory analysis.

cited_work_check.title: Free View Synthesis (Riegler & Koltun, ECCV 2020)
cited_work_check.note: Confirmed: empirical learned IBR on MVS proxy geometry, with no analytic treatment.

cited_work_check.title: Plenoptic Sampling (Chai et al., SIGGRAPH 2000)
cited_work_check.note: A classic; I did not reopen the page. The characterisation is accurate. The ideator omits closer classic theory: Lin & Shum's geometric analysis of light-field rendering (IJCV 2004) and Pujades et al. (CVPR 2014).

cited_work_check.title: Unstructured Lumigraph Rendering (Buehler et al., SIGGRAPH 2001)
cited_work_check.note: The 'heuristics' characterisation is correct. But Pujades et al., CVPR 2014, already derived these heuristics from an explicit geometric-uncertainty error model, and the ideator missed it.

cited_work_check.title: 3DTV: A Feedforward Interpolation Network for Real-Time View Synthesis (2026)
cited_work_check.note: Exists. It is a hybrid of lightweight geometry and learning, and its abstract has no when-geometry-helps analysis. It is valid as a baseline only.

threats.title: Bayesian View Synthesis and Image-Based Rendering Principles (Pujades, Devernay, Goldluecke)
threats.what_overlaps: A physics-based generative model of IBR that systematically accounts for the error induced by uncertainty in the geometric proxy. It derives blending weights (a MAP estimate) and explains the ULR heuristics analytically. This covers the 'error propagation from geometry uncertainty into K-view blending' core and directly undercuts the claim that ULR-style blending has only heuristics.
threats.what_remains_different: It is static and single-frame, with no temporal depth-noise statistics, no flicker, no learned renderers or crossover analysis, and no temporal filter or TSDF analysis.

threats.title: An Analytical Model for Synthesis Distortion Estimation in 3D Video (Fang, Cheung, Au, et al.)
threats.what_overlaps: An analytical model of how depth error propagates into synthesized-view distortion, as a function of texture characteristics (the frequency and gradient content of the texture) and the geometry of the view shift. This is essentially the Δu·||∇I|| first-order model.
threats.what_remains_different: It targets depth-coding rate allocation for 2-view DIBR, not K-view learned blending. There is no temporal bias/variance split, no flicker prediction and no comparison with learned renderers.

threats.title: Depth map distortion analysis for view rendering and depth coding (Kim, Ortega, et al.)
threats.what_overlaps: Derives rendered-view error from depth error times local texture gradient, scaled by camera parameters and baseline. This is the same first-order displacement-times-gradient relation as the idea's key insight.
threats.what_remains_different: Static, used for compression. It has no temporal statistics, no multi-view blending, no TSDF or filter analysis and no learned renderers.

threats.title: Estimation of Virtual View Synthesis Distortion Toward Virtual View Position
threats.what_overlaps: Models how synthesis distortion from depth error scales with the virtual-view position (the effective baseline), matching the idea's b_eff term.
threats.what_remains_different: No temporal dimension, no learned blending and no geometry-versus-learned crossover.

threats.title: A Low-Complexity View Synthesis Distortion Estimation Method for 3D Video with Large Baseline Considerations (Bi & Liang)
threats.what_overlaps: Recent (Oct 2025) training-free view synthesis distortion (VSD) estimation with a baseline-distance indicator, texture-depth region classification, and region-based blending including overlap and disocclusion regions. It shows this line is still active and covers the occlusion and disocclusion term the idea lists as a risk.
threats.what_remains_different: Frame-level distortion estimation for 3D video coding. It has no temporal flicker model, no bias/variance split and no learned renderers.

threats.title: A Geometric Analysis of Light Field Rendering (Lin & Shum)
threats.what_overlaps: Analytic bounds on rendering quality (blur and ghosting) as a function of depth uncertainty and camera spacing. This is a rig-design theory that predates the idea's 'rig-design calculator'.
threats.what_remains_different: Static light fields with no temporal noise, flicker or learned renderers.

threats.title: Subjective and Objective Video Quality Assessment of 3D Synthesized Views With Texture/Depth Compression Distortion (Liu et al.)
threats.what_overlaps: Treats temporal flicker from temporally inconsistent depth as a distinct distortion from spatial error in DIBR-synthesized video, with metrics for each. This is the empirical counterpart of the idea's claim that flicker comes from temporal variance and fidelity from bias. A related paper, 'Measurement of critical temporal inconsistency for quality assessment of synthesized video' (ICIP 2016, doi 10.1109/ICIP.2016.7532513), does the same.
threats.what_remains_different: Empirical QA with no analytic propagation, no multi-view learned blending and no temporal-filter or TSDF theory.

threats.title: Depth No-Synthesis-Error Model for View Synthesis in 3-D Video (D-NOSE)
threats.what_overlaps: Characterises the depth-error tolerance below which rounding in DIBR causes no synthesis error, and has been used to smooth depth temporally and suppress flicker.
threats.what_remains_different: An integer-disparity rounding model only. It has no bias/variance temporal theory and no learned renderers.

threats.title: Learning Dynamic View Synthesis With Few RGBD Cameras
threats.what_overlaps: Identifies unstable depth as the cause of flicker and ghosting in RGB-D dynamic view synthesis and adds temporal stabilisation.
threats.what_remains_different: A method paper with no theory.

novelty.best_variant: There is only one idea in C18. Its defensible part is contributions 1 and 2: the temporal bias/variance split (fidelity versus flicker), which explains why depth-consistency machinery improves temporal metrics but not PSNR, and the geometry-versus-learned crossover condition, validated by controlled sweeps. These extend Fang 2014, Kim & Ortega 2009 and Pujades 2014, which the ideator missed, into the temporal domain and to learned renderers. The GAI router and rig calculator should be presented as applications, not as core novelty.

sharpened.title: A Flicker Budget for Geometry-Guided View Synthesis: Temporal Bias-Variance Propagation of Depth Error, and When Learned Renderers Win
sharpened.one_liner: We extend classic static models of DIBR synthesis distortion to time and to learned renderers. The extended model predicts per-pixel fidelity error and flicker from depth-error statistics, and it predicts where geometry-guided and learned renderers cross over. Two design tools follow from it: a Kalman-optimal temporal depth filter and a rig/sensor flicker calculator.
sharpened.core_claim: Split per-pixel depth error into a temporally static bias and an AR(1)-correlated fluctuation (variance sigma_nu^2, correlation rho), and add a visibility-flip term at occlusions. A closed-form first-order model then does two things. (i) It predicts measured frame MSE and frame-difference flicker energy of K-view warp-and-blend renderers with R^2 >= 0.8 across more than 1000 controlled configurations on synthetic data and on real ActorsHQ images, while static distortion models (Kim-Ortega 2009, Fang 2014) predict flicker with R^2 < 0.5. (ii) It predicts the PSNR change and the STED/warping-error change caused by temporal filtering and TSDF fusion: PSNR gain is roughly 10log10((b^2+v)/(b^2+gamma*v)), which is near zero when bias dominates, while flicker scales roughly with gamma*(1-rho_eff)*v. The model explains the base paper's ablation pattern (no PSNR change, large STED change) within seed variance. (iii) Given each renderer's two measured quantities, its bias map and its noise-transfer gain, it predicts the depth-noise level sigma_z* at which a geometry-guided renderer stops beating a learned or geometry-free renderer, within a factor of 1.5 on at least 75% of held-out configurations. Any one of these failing falsifies the claim.
sharpened.key_insight: PSNR and flicker metrics measure different moments of the same error process. Frame MSE is bias^2 + variance. Frame-difference metrics (STED, flow-warping error, TCC) see only the decorrelated part of the variance, 2(1-rho)v, plus view-set switching. Depth-consistency machinery (EMA filter, TSDF, previous-frame feedback) is a variance reducer with a computable gain gamma and never touches bias. So it is expected to be invisible to PSNR whenever bias^2 >> v, which is the base paper's case. Renderers can then be compared by two measurable quantities rather than by architecture. A geometry-guided warp is low-bias but high-gain: its gain scales with ||grad I|| * f * b_eff / z^2. Learned and geometry-free renderers are higher-bias (blur toward the conditional mean) and lower-gain. That gives a closed-form crossover sigma_z*^2 = (b_L^2 + V_L - b_G^2)/G_G^2 per pixel class. The same decomposition gives the minimum-variance temporal filter gain per pixel, which replaces the hand-set floor M >= 0.6.
sharpened.method: THEORY. The target colour is I_hat(x,t) = sum_k w_k I_k(pi_k(X + eps_k)). Linearise around the true surface. The per-view displacement is du_k = J_k eps_k, with ||J_k|| ~ f*b_eff,k/z^2 including a slant term. Per-view depth error is eps_k(x,t) = beta_k(x) + nu_k(x,t), where nu is AR(1) with (sigma_nu, rho) and the cross-view correlation c is an explicit parameter; c matters because TSDF averaging only helps if view errors are decorrelated. Closed forms: E[e^2] = bias^2 + v; flicker energy F = E[(e_t - e_{t-1})^2] = 2(1-rho)v + a K-set switching term for moving viewers. Three extra terms are added. (a) Occlusions: a Bernoulli visibility-flip term p(1-p)*Delta_c^2, with p = Phi(depth_gap/sigma_z). (b) View dependence: a colour discrepancy that grows with source-target angle times specular lobe sharpness. (c) Operators: EMA filter with mask floor alpha gives gamma_EMA = alpha/(2-alpha) * (1+(1-alpha)rho)/(1-(1-alpha)rho); the image-based TSDF is weighted averaging over K views with truncation clipping; the learned blend weights are treated as fixed per pixel, since their temporal variation is measured separately. LEARNED RENDERERS are characterised empirically rather than abstracted. The bias map comes from GT-depth or clean inputs versus GT images. The noise-transfer gain G comes from finite-difference or JVP probing of the output with respect to input depth and image perturbations (Hutchinson estimate, about 32 probes per frame). The intrinsic temporal variance V_L comes from identical-input jitter. This covers ENeRF, GPS-Gaussian, IBRNet and a small geometry-free LVSM-class model trained on the same data. PARAMETER ESTIMATION on real data: sigma_nu, rho and c are fitted from real stereo and ToF streams (RAFT-Stereo, FoundationStereo-class, Stereo Any Video, Kinect) against mesh GT on ActorsHQ and against static-region statistics on DyNeRF. APPLICATIONS, which are derived and not the core novelty. (1) A per-pixel minimum-MSE temporal filter (a scalar Kalman gain from the estimated v, motion probability and rho) as a drop-in replacement for the base paper's colour-difference EMA, costing under 1 ms per frame on GPU. (2) A rig/sensor flicker calculator: given sigma_z(z) (stereo sigma_z = z^2 sigma_d/(f B), or a ToF model), camera count, baseline and viewer volume, it outputs a predicted fidelity/flicker map and a minimum K or camera density for a flicker target. (3) An optional per-pixel crossover map (the former Geometry Advantage Index) for routing between geometry-guided and learned outputs. Only (1) and (2) are headline results. Analysis is offline; the only runtime component is filter (1).
sharpened.why_not_engineering: The deliverable is a predictive, falsifiable model with closed forms, not a pipeline tweak. It makes quantitative predictions before any experiment is run: the PSNR change and flicker change from a filter, the crossover sigma_z*, and the minimum camera count for a flicker target. It resolves an observed inconsistency in the literature: consistency machinery improves temporal metrics and leaves PSNR unchanged, and TCC is insensitive. It also turns two hand-tuned heuristics, the mask floor and the fixed K, into derived quantities. The test is whether measured numbers fall on predicted curves across more than 1000 configurations and several renderer families. That is the standard of an analysis paper, not a systems paper.
sharpened.differentiation: Kim & Ortega (ICIP 2009), Fang et al. (TIP 2014), the TIP 2016 virtual-view-position model and Bi & Liang (arXiv 2510.17037) model static synthesized-view distortion as depth error times texture gradient times baseline, for 2-view DIBR coding. We cite them as our first-order building block and add temporal statistics (bias vs AR(1) variance, cross-view correlation, K-set switching), occlusion flips, K-view learned blending and learned renderers. We show experimentally that their static models cannot predict flicker. Pujades et al. (CVPR 2014) derive blending weights from geometric uncertainty for a single static frame; we are temporal, and we derive filter gains rather than blending weights. Lin & Shum (IJCV 2004) and Plenoptic Sampling are static sampling bounds; our rig calculator targets temporal flicker budgets under a real sensor noise model. Liu et al. (TIP 2015) and the temporal IV-PSNR metric separate flicker from spatial distortion empirically; we supply the generative account that explains why each metric responds to which error moment. LVSM, SVSM and the 'From Rays to Projections' paper (arXiv 2601.05116, checked) argue for less 3D bias empirically on static benchmarks, with no temporal analysis and no crossover analysis. The base paper (arXiv 2505.18932) and 3DTV (arXiv 2604.11211) are instances analysed by the model.

datasets: Synthetic controlled suite rendered with Blender or Kubric: animated humans and objects with GT depth, normals and a BRDF roughness sweep, virtual rigs of 4-24 cameras, baselines 0.1-1 m, injected depth noise with controlled bias, sigma_nu, rho and cross-view correlation. More than 1000 configurations; the main validation bed.

ActorsHQ (HumanRF, arXiv 2305.06356; verified 160 cams, 12 MP, per-frame mesh reconstructions): real images with mesh-derived depth. Subsample cameras to emulate 4-16-camera telepresence rigs. Real-image validation with near-GT geometry.

DyNeRF / Neural 3D Video: replicate the base paper's TSDF and temporal-filter ablations with multiple seeds and test the predicted PSNR and STED changes. Real stereo depth, no GT depth, so static-region statistics are used.
ENeRF-Outdoor: the large-z, far-background regime. Test the predicted crossover where ENeRF beats the geometry-guided pipeline (base paper Table 2).
DNA-Rendering and/or MVHumanNet: humans with clothing specularity and many views, for the view-dependent term and the generalisation of learned-renderer probing. Check licence and download access.
CMU Panoptic Kinect subset: real ToF sensor noise statistics for the rig/sensor calculator. Verify that the synchronised Kinect streams and calibration are still downloadable.
D3DMV (the base paper's third dataset), optional for completeness.
baselines: Re-implementation of the base pipeline in stages: distance blending, then + learned blend net, + temporal filter, + image-based TSDF, + previous-frame feedback. No official code exists, so re-implementation is required.
ENeRF (depth-guided learned renderer)
GPS-Gaussian (pixel-aligned Gaussian, human rigs)
IBRNet (learned IBR)
Geometry-free LVSM-class renderer (Efficient-LVSM or a small LVSM/SVSM retrained on the same synthetic and ActorsHQ data at 256-512 px)
3DTV (arXiv 2604.11211) if code is available

Predictor baselines: static distortion models (Kim-Ortega 2009; Fang et al. TIP 2014), Pujades 2014 uncertainty weights, and a learned no-reference flicker predictor (small CNN trained on the same features) as an upper-bound check for the theory
Filter baselines: the base paper's colour-difference EMA (M >= 0.6), a fixed-gain Kalman filter, and a post-hoc video deflickering method applied to renderer outputs
metrics: Predicted-vs-measured R^2 and regression slope for frame MSE, bias^2, variance and flicker energy, per region (visible, occlusion boundary, disoccluded)
Crossover prediction: |log(sigma_z*_pred / sigma_z*_meas)| and the fraction within a factor of 1.5
Fidelity: PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS
Temporal: STED, TCC (as in the base paper), flow-based warping error (Lai et al. 2018), temporal IV-PSNR, and x-t slice variance
Filter application: STED and warping error at matched PSNR, plus ms per frame
Rig calculator: predicted vs measured minimum camera count for a flicker target on camera subsets of ActorsHQ and DyNeRF
All real-data results over at least 3 seeds with confidence intervals
key_ablations: First-order visible-only model vs + occlusion visibility-flip term vs + view-dependent term: how much variance each term explains, per region
i.i.d. temporal noise vs AR(1) (rho) vs AR(1) + cross-view correlation c (tests the TSDF-helps-only-if-decorrelated prediction)
Static viewer vs moving viewer, with and without the K-set switching term
Learned renderer characterised by bias only vs bias + gain vs bias + gain + intrinsic variance
Noise from synthetic injection vs real stereo/ToF estimators with fitted parameters (does the theory transfer to structured real errors?)
Theory-optimal per-pixel filter gain vs base-paper heuristic vs oracle GT-tuned gain
Sensitivity of predictions to mis-estimated sigma_nu and rho (robustness of the calculator)
experiments.capture_notes: No custom capture is needed for the core paper. Synthetic scenes give full control. ActorsHQ gives real images with mesh GT depth. DyNeRF, ENeRF-Outdoor and DNA-Rendering cover the real-renderer regimes. Panoptic Kinect supplies real ToF noise. An optional small rig (4-6 cameras plus 1-2 stereo or ToF sensors, about 2 weeks) would strengthen the rig-calculator claim with a prospective test: predict the camera count needed for a flicker target, then build it and measure. Worthwhile only if a journal or IEEE VR version wants a hardware validation.

review.first_two_week_test:
Week 1. On two ActorsHQ sequences (8-camera subset, 100 frames, depth rendered from the provided meshes) and one Blender scene with an animated character, implement a minimal K=4 forward warp-and-blend renderer with angle/distance weights and an optional EMA filter. Pure PyTorch; about 3 days. Inject depth noise eps = beta + nu(t) on a grid: sigma_beta and sigma_nu each in {0, 0.5, 1, 2, 4} cm, rho in {0, 0.5, 0.9}, three baselines, with and without EMA (alpha = 0.6). That is about 150 configurations of minutes each on one GPU. Compute closed-form predictions of MSE, bias^2, variance and flicker energy per pixel from GT gradients, b_eff and z. Report R^2 by region.

Week 2. (a) Test the headline prediction. For each configuration, predict the PSNR change and flicker change from turning the EMA on, and compare with measurement. The target pattern is the base paper's: PSNR change under 0.1 dB with a large flicker drop when bias^2/v > 3. (b) Probe a pretrained GPS-Gaussian (human rig), or ENeRF, with finite-difference depth and image perturbations to estimate its bias and gain on the same frames. Predict sigma_z* and compare with the measured crossover along the noise sweep. (c) Fit a Fang/Kim-Ortega static model as a baseline predictor of flicker.

Go if: flicker R^2 >= 0.8 in visible regions and >= 0.65 overall; predicted filter PSNR change within 0.2 dB and flicker change within 25%; the static model is clearly worse on flicker (R^2 lower by at least 0.25); and GPS-Gaussian's measured gain is stable (CV < 30%) across frames.
review.kill_criteria: Kill, or demote to a workshop note, if any of the following holds. (1) Flicker R^2 < 0.6 even in visible regions, meaning the first-order temporal model is not predictive. (2) Occlusion-boundary and disocclusion pixels carry more than 60% of flicker energy and the Bernoulli visibility-flip term does not raise overall R^2 above 0.65. (3) The static Fang/Kim-Ortega model with a naive per-frame variance plug-in predicts flicker as well as ours (R^2 gap < 0.1); the temporal extension is then trivial and the novelty collapses into prior art. (4) Learned renderers' noise-transfer gain or bias varies so much across scenes or frames (CV > 50%) that the crossover prediction misses by more than 2x on over half of configurations. (5) With real stereo errors on ActorsHQ, the fitted AR(1)+bias model explains under 50% of the measured error autocovariance. (6) The theory-optimal filter fails to beat the base-paper heuristic on flow-warping error at matched PSNR, removing the practical payoff. (7) A concurrent paper (check the MPEG MIV/immersive-video and coding literature, which prior searches could not fully cover because APIs were rate-limited) already publishes a temporal bias/variance synthesis-distortion model with flicker prediction.

reviewer_objections.objection: The core propagation model, displacement ~ f*b*eps/z^2 times the texture gradient, is textbook DIBR distortion modelling (Kim-Ortega 2009, Fang TIP 2014, Pujades CVPR 2014). This is a rehash.
reviewer_objections.rebuttal: We cite these works as the first-order building block and claim none of it. The contributions are the temporal moments (bias vs AR(1) variance, cross-view correlation, K-set switching), the operator gains of filters and TSDF, occlusion flips, and the learned-renderer crossover. A head-to-head experiment shows static models predict flicker with R^2 below 0.5 against 0.8 or more for ours, and cannot explain the PSNR/STED dissociation.

reviewer_objections.objection: Linearisation breaks exactly where errors live: occlusion boundaries, disocclusions, thin structures and specular surfaces.
reviewer_objections.rebuttal: The model includes an explicit visibility-flip (Bernoulli) term and a view-dependent term. Results report explained variance per region (visible, boundary, disoccluded), so readers see where the theory holds and where it degrades. The kill criterion is pre-registered: if boundaries dominate and the flip term fails, we say so.

reviewer_objections.objection: You cannot meaningfully 'model' a learned or geometry-free transformer with a toy estimator; the crossover claim is hand-waving.
reviewer_objections.rebuttal: We do not abstract learned renderers. Each one is characterised empirically by three measured quantities: its bias map, its noise-transfer gain from JVP or finite-difference probing, and its intrinsic temporal variance. The theory needs only these to predict the crossover sigma_z*, which is then checked on held-out noise levels and scenes for four renderer families.

reviewer_objections.objection: Synthetic i.i.d. or AR(1) depth noise is unrealistic; real stereo errors are structured, edge-aligned and content-dependent.
reviewer_objections.rebuttal: Noise parameters are fitted from real estimators (RAFT-Stereo, a FoundationStereo-class model, Stereo Any Video, Kinect ToF) against mesh GT on ActorsHQ, including spatially varying bias maps. A dedicated ablation compares injected and real-estimator errors. The theory consumes per-pixel statistics, not a global noise model.

reviewer_objections.objection: An analysis paper with no new SOTA method; the motivating puzzle rests on a single unreplicated ablation.
reviewer_objections.rebuttal: We re-run the ablation with multiple seeds; the theory's predictions do not depend on the puzzle being large. Two concrete payoffs come from the theory: a per-pixel minimum-MSE temporal filter that lowers warping error at matched PSNR at under 1 ms cost, and a rig/sensor calculator validated on camera subsets. Both are practical tools that telepresence builders currently lack.

effort.months: 6-8 (2 for the theory plus the 2-week gate, 2-3 for base-pipeline re-implementation and renderer probing, 2 for real-data validation, the filter and the rig calculator)
effort.people: 1 PhD student with a strong math and statistics background, plus 0.5 of a second person for renderer re-implementation, retraining and the synthetic data generator
effort.compute: 2-4 GPUs (24-80 GB) for sweeps and probing; about 1-2 weeks on 4-8 A100-class GPUs to retrain a small LVSM-class geometry-free model at 256-512 px. Synthetic rendering on a CPU/GPU farm, around 1-2 TB of storage.

review.venue: Primary: ICCV 2027 (deadline around March 2027), framed as an analysis paper with the theory-optimal filter and rig calculator as validated applications. CVPR 2027 (November 2026) is too early to run the full validation. Fallbacks: 3DV 2028, or IEEE TVCG (journal, or the IEEE VR/ISMAR journal tracks), where a rig-design angle for telepresence is valued and a theory-heavy paper with thorough validation fares well. The full version with the renderer crossover and rig calculator fits TPAMI.
review.synergies: (1) Uncertainty-aware depth fusion and temporally consistent video stereo (Stereo Any Video, streaming geometry foundation models): the theory says which error moment to reduce (decorrelated variance vs bias) and gives the Kalman gain, so it could be the analysis section of a method paper on learned temporal depth filtering. (2) Temporal-consistency benchmarks and metrics: it explains why PSNR and TCC are blind to consistency machinery, which justifies a new flicker-sensitive metric suite such as warping error or temporal IV-PSNR. (3) Hybrid geometry-guided transformer renderers (LVSM/SVSM with TSDF priors): the crossover map indicates where to spend neural compute or route pixels. (4) Compression-aware RGB-D telepresence: codec-induced depth noise enters as nu with a known spectrum, enabling bit allocation for a flicker target. (5) Moving and binocular viewers: the K-set switching term predicts view-change flicker and left/right inconsistency. (6) Confidence-gated generative fixers: predicted per-pixel variance and bias act as a free, principled confidence signal. Best packaging is a two-paper series. Paper A is this analysis with the optimal filter. Paper B is a method paper (learned temporal state or uncertainty-aware fusion) that uses paper A's predictions as design rationale and evaluation protocol.
